en: Regarding the *Detailed Explanation of the Essential Commentary on the Ten Non-dual Gates*:
this work clarifies the intent of Jingxi [Zhanran] and skillfully demonstrates the essentials of cultivation and realization.
It was composed by Master Wujie, who provided a thorough and exhaustive commentary; its meaning is meticulous and it has rendered great service.

Regarding the student editions, there were those whose collations were not entirely excellent; moreover, as the national edition contained many errors and omissions, students at the elementary level often suffered from these defects.
(I), having previously sought out and obtained a superior copy, collated it once against the others and privately corrected those parts of the collation that were imperfect.
Yet, fearing that my work might still not be exhaustive, I have delayed carving the woodblocks until last autumn.
Based on the lecture notes from the original temple, I have once again meticulously collated and edited this work, consulting with senior masters and veteran monks before carving it for circulation.
Since the language is easy to understand, readers will likely develop profound insights;
thus, I hope this undertaking may serve as a small aid toward establishing one's practice and cultivating spiritual realization.
On the first day of the eighth month of autumn in the year of Guiwei of the Genroku era,
the śramaṇa Ryōjun of Tiantai Mountain composed this preface within King Tokugawa’s Enlightenment Hall (En-gaku-shitsu).
Preface to the Detailed Commentary on the *Essential Excerpts on the Ten Non-Dual Gates* (Nine Articles): 1.
Regarding errors present in the National Edition, I have now collated and corrected them all according to the Ming edition.
Where there were doubtful or erroneous characters in the Ming edition, I have noted "character X is suspected" above the corresponding grid.

First, regarding the *Shiqian* and the *Chao*, there have been various editions that differ from those currently combined here; these are noted by stating, "one edition has such-and-such a character" or "one edition reads such-and-such a character.
Second, as for the *Huiben*, at the beginning of each fascicle, the author lists the names of the two patriarchs directly by their posthumous titles; this is not a way to show them due respect.
The patriarchs have now all deleted these [titles] and retained only the designation "Venerable So-and-so.
As for the headings of the topical explanations (shìtí) marked in the original assembly texts, these are neither the headings of the *Chāo* nor are they explanatory text;

rather, they were privately added at the time of dividing the assemblies with the intention of corresponding to the headings of the explanatory text. Now, I wish to avoid confusing these with the headings of the *Chāo*.
Delete all of this.

It is highly improper that the single edition does not list the names of those who composed the *Zhǐyào* (Essential Points) and the *Shùshì* (Explanations), yet instead lists the names of those who composed the *Shìqiān* (Sub-commentary). This contradicts the intent of the *Jiàochě* (Commentary).
Now, based on the *Jiàochě*, we shall determine whether the inclusion or exclusion [of these names] is appropriate.
In the original edition of the *Biaobiao Ke*, certain figures were deleted from various sections and characters and phrases were frequently altered or excised;
now, based on the original text, all have been fully restored so that not a single character has been lost.
Although there may indeed be principles for supplementing the sections on the "Concluding the Assembly" (*jie-men*) from various private sources, one must not add them arbitrarily.
Here, I have instead separately marked the various precedents above to facilitate the observation of the sequential correspondence between preceding and following passages.
Regarding the errors in the collation of this first edition, there are three places that have now all been corrected.
First, in this re-engraving, the primary aim was to revise and supplement the collated edition so that its additions and deletions would fully reflect the original texts of each work.

However, while the *Shiqian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning) and the *Zhijue yaochao* (Essential Notes on the Profound Meaning) exist as separate editions and can be consulted for verification, the *Jiangyi* (Detailed Explanation) does not exist as a separate edition.
Because it has been lost for a long time, there are now many points that are questionable and cannot be verified through comparison; let the reader examine this matter with care.
Preface to the Detailed Commentary on the *Essential Excerpts of the Ten Non-dual Gates* (Shibuermen zhiyao chao xiangjie xu).
The *Zhijyao Chao* (Essential Commentary on the Tenfold Non-duality) is the wondrous key that opens the gates of the "Tenfold Non-duality. Its language is profound and its meaning is deep;

were it not for those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom, how could one penetrate it? The Great Master Wujie Ke Du of the Song dynasty, who deeply understood the teachings and contemplations of this school, composed a detailed commentary upon it.
This was truly like using an axe handle to split firewood or wielding a blade with such mastery that it splits bamboo as if it were a stalk of reed. However, its original text...

The text was refined but remained incomplete, a source of frustration for students. Master Yunshi of Tiantai was a high disciple of Great Master Wujin; his elder brother, Master Yuan, was likewise a great figure in the Dharma-gate.
Whenever they recalled this work, they would often clench their fists in regret. Consequently, Master Yunshi devoted himself to collating and harmonizing the fragments into a complete volume.
Before it could be published, he passed away. Master Yun, lamenting that his elder brother’s aspirations had remained unfulfilled, was resolute in his resolve.
Nevertheless, would it not be excellent to carry on his intent and carve [this work] into blocks for the public and his fellow students? Alas!

If this commentary circulates, the Tiantai school will become as bright as the sun and stars. If one reads these volumes together with undivided focus, the great purport of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s "opening and merging" (*kaie*) will be understood by more than half; is this not a great service to future learners? This cannot be denied.
One day, the Assistant Administrator (Cheng) solicited donations to entrust to the carvers for printing. Upon its completion, he requested a preface from me.
I was ashamed that I lacked literary talent, yet I have straightforwardly recounted the details of this collaborative carving and the earnest efforts of the brothers involved.
Thus it is said.
Written by the later disciple of Tiantai from Wulin, the śramaṇa Haiyan, on the second day after the Dragon Boat Festival in the year of Xinchwei during the Chongzhen reign, at Baoguo Monastery.
General Preface to the Detailed Commentary on the *Essentials of the Ten Non-Dual Gates*.

Now, those who possess the wondrous mind are humans; those who awaken to the wondrous mind are Buddhas; those who expound the wondrous mind are the Teachings; and those who interpret the wondrous Teachings are the Patriarchs.
Since the words of the Patriarchs are profound and mysterious, one must enter through their gateways. Although the wondrous gateways have been opened, one must grasp the essential point to ascend.

Once the essential point is indicated as something upon which to rely, it is only through detailed explanation that understanding begins. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is that which expounds the wondrous mind.
This ultimate teaching clarifies the Buddha’s profound and subtle exposition; the Tathāgata preached it over eight years, and the Council compiled it into eight thousand *li* of Sanskrit volumes.
Its transmission is like a single grain of millet from a great granary, and Kumārajīva’s translation is like a single bubble upon the vast ocean.
Yet, by condensing one *kalpa* into a single day, the wondrous power of the *Ṣaḍabhijñā-kośa* (Treasury of Supernatural Powers) encompasses the oceans of lands within a single pore.
The profound mystery arises from the ultimate principle; thus, even a single grain of millet can serve as the seed for a great granary, and a single bubble can encompass the depths of the vast ocean.
That the Seven Buddhas were masters who expounded the sutras and that the sixty thousand [patriarchs] transmitted the mind—these words are not erroneous, and their meaning may be verified.
Now, when one tastes a single grain, all flavors are present therein; when one beholds a single bubble, [the entire ocean is revealed].
If both the oceans and the seas are present, they can only be found within our Tiantai Master Zhizhe, who possesses the five tongues and five eyes;
indeed, it is only he who can attain them. For the Master heard the teachings at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in former lives and attained wondrous awakening at the Great Su Mountain;

with unimpeded eloquence, he proclaimed the Dharma in accordance with its nature. Relying on the two gates of the trace and the source, he revealed the two wonders of the "waiting" and the "transcendent," thereby fulfilling the great task of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the Buddha’s knowledge and vision concerning sentient beings, at this point there is likely nothing further remaining.

However, as the Section on Traces is not remote from the Ten Profound Subtleties (*daśa-prakarṣa*), the ultimate principle is difficult to penetrate; though the sublime mind is manifest, it is difficult to awaken to.

For this reason, Jingxi opened the way with the *Ten Gates of Non-duality*, and Siming pointed to the essential point of the single thought-moment. Alas! If one is like the Tathāgata or a wise person, one may be said to have shattered [all delusions].
A single mote of dust gives rise to a great chiliocosm of sutra scrolls; thus, Jingxi and Siming may be said to have merged the great chiliocosm of sutra scrolls back into a single mote of dust.

Therefore, the *Fahua Xuanyi Jimen Shimiao Shibunimon Shiyao Chao* is truly the essential gateway for directly pointing to the human mind and seeing one's nature to achieve Buddhahood, wherein there is no departure from the written word.

It is here that the secret canon of liberation is expounded; taking the concise as the source of the vast and the brief as the foundation of the detailed, who else could have transmitted the refined meaning of the Four Ming (Siming Fazhi) teachings except for the Great Master Keduo of Qiantang?

He brought forth a detailed commentary of over one hundred thousand words, much like the royal house’s chamber of pepper: were it not for the master of the vermilion gate and the jar, its depths and shallows would remain unknown.
It is not that those who guard the gates fail to open its steps for him; rather, it is because his excellent grace has been left behind for posterity and his fragrance flows on through later times.

It is a pity that he did not enter the Great Canon, but instead his works were scattered among the monastic quarters; thus, while we may look up to his illustrious name, we have not had the opportunity to set our eyes upon them.
There was a monk from Yanqing Temple in Siling named Hui, whose courtesy name was Langchu; he was a monk of poetry and wine who happened, by chance, [to encounter...]
Although this mountain temple obtained this book, though we knew the well contained treasure, we did not understand how to light a torch to observe it.
We presented it to you for use as a pure offering. You received it like one parched with thirst drinking a full draught of nectar, or like one famished satiated by the finest clarified butter;

we hope you will ascend to the heights of the *li* and *zao* fruits to share it with those of like mind. Furthermore, we have separately circulated a commentary and sub-commentary, though they are difficult to master.
I have searched through and collated this text with my disciples Zhengmi and Zhenghui, compiling it and storing it within a chest for thirty years.

Now, my disciple Zhengshi has made a firm and sincere resolve to sponsor its carving into woodblocks; thus, the conditions have converged and the Great Dharma is destined to spread. Seeing this in my advanced age, I am truly filled with joy.
Nevertheless, the source of this merit is not of my own making; the wise monks were certainly instrumental in providing the causes and conditions. From this, it can be seen that...

I repent for the transgression of frivolous speech throughout my life—the sin of having my tongue cut off—and I expiate the offenses of the yeast-and-malt vats and the river of ashes accumulated over kalpas.

By this, may I receive profound benefit in the afterlife and truly become a monk. Through the truth of my words, I shall praise the doctrine of the inherent nature; through the wisdom of my deeds, I shall tear asunder the net of delusion and ignorance.
May these merits be universally bestowed upon the four modes of birth, so that both self and others may together attain the ten wonders. This is how I may repay [my debts].
This is the mountain monk’s aspiration for its circulation and the filial resolve of his two disciples.
Recorded in the winter of the fifth year of the Ming Tianqi era, the year of Yichou (1625), by the śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi on Mount Tiantai.

Preface to the *Fenhuì Zhīyào Chāo* by Zhengmi, a Later Disciple of Tiantai. [Commentary]:
The first three characters of this title refer to the main text being prefaced; the character "xu" (preface) is the general term for that which performs the prefacing.

Because the specific is used to distinguish it from the general, it is called the "Preface to the *Zhīyào Chāo*. As for the two characters "zhīyào" (essential points), they refer to the essential points [of the text].
Regarding the preface to the *Xizicao* (Western Aid Commentary), which was compiled by the author himself as a record of its own commentary:

"Now, the existence of commentaries (*ji*) upon exegeses (*shu*), and the compilation of records of essential meanings and the transcription of wise sayings, serve to support those exegeses, to prevent errors in oral transmission, and to remedy forgetfulness during study. (Text) A preface is for this purpose..."

The meaning of the term "xu" (preface/introduction) is as follows: The *Erya* states, "The walls on the east and west are called xu," with the commentary noting that they serve to distinguish between the interior and exterior.
(Textually: This refers to seeing how the walls demarcate the depth of a residence; by observing the xu, one knows the ease or difficulty of the composition.
Furthermore, "xu" means a thread or sequence, referring to the thread of a cocoon. In all cases, when drawing silk from a cocoon, one first draws [the inner thread].
Only when the strands are completely exhausted does one see the thread; the present preface stands at the beginning like the strand of a thread (Kuangji).
[Preface] Composed by the Śramaṇa Zunshe of Mount Dōsan. [Commentary] Mount Dōsan is Mount Tōyaku in Tai (Tiantai), at the monastery of Nōnin-ji.
The Ritual Master says: "Mount Tōyaku is indeed the place where I received the scriptures in my youth, and the site where the Dharma was transmitted during that time.
The Ritual Master’s clan name is Ye; he is a native of Ninghai in Tai. His mother sought spiritual protection...
In a dream, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva appeared as a beautiful woman who gave him a bright pearl; he swallowed it and was born seven months later.
At seven months of age, he could recite the name of Avalokiteśvara from his mother’s lips. At eighteen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination.
He initially resided at Baoyun Monastery and eventually traveled to India. Together with Fazhi, he studied under Master Baotongyun, and thus the *Yiji* (Essential Points) was completed.
He then composed a preface to elucidate the merit of this work of exposition. A śramaṇa remarked: "Regarding 'exposition,' the *Li* says:
'The expositor is called enlightened; the author is called sage. To speak now of 'exposition' is likely a term of humility.
As the saying goes: 'I transmit but do not create.'"

**[Preface]** The flourishing of the Great Teaching in the lands of the Yi depends upon its individuals. Since the various patriarchs have passed away, the profound transformation has nearly ceased; time cannot endure such a lapse, and there must inevitably appear those who emerge at intervals between eras. **[Commentary]** This general account of the rise and decline of the teachings depends upon individuals. "The Great Teaching" refers generally to the Buddha-dharma; the *General Preface* states that the Great Dharma gradually spread to the East, while the *Zhuan* (Sub-commentary) says: ... [text continues] ... **[General Account of the Rise and Decline of the Teachings]** The Buddha-dharma first appeared in China during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han. It was propagated by the two masters, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, and subsequently flourished through the efforts of the three translators, including An Shigao. During the Wei, Jin, and Northern and Southern Dynasties, the teachings were further disseminated by figures such as Kumārajīva, Bodhiruci, Paramārtha, Xuanzang, and Amoghavajra.

However, from the Tang dynasty onward, the world fell into turmoil, and the Buddhist community suffered greatly. During the Five Dynasties period, the Dharma declined even further. It was only with the advent of the Song dynasty that the teachings were revived. Subsequently, during the Yuan and Ming dynasties, the situation remained precarious. It was not until the early years of the Qing dynasty that the Dharma began to flourish once again. This brief history of the rise and fall of the teachings is intended to provide a general overview for the sake of future generations. Although the Dharma has been transmitted for over a thousand years, it has experienced periods of both prosperity and decline. It is essential that those who uphold the teachings remain vigilant and strive to ensure its continued survival. May this record serve as a reminder for all who seek to propagate the Way. **[General Overview of the Flourishing of the Great Teaching]** The flourishing of the Great Teaching in the lands of the Yi depends entirely upon the individuals who carry it forth. Since the various patriarchs have passed away, the profound transformation has nearly ceased; time cannot endure such a lapse, and there must inevitably appear those who emerge at intervals between eras. Regarding the term "Great Teaching," this refers generally to the Buddha-dharma. As the *General Preface* states that the Great Dharma gradually spread to the East, and the *Zhuan* notes that the Buddha-dharma first appeared in China during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han, it is clear that the transmission of the Dharma across the ages relies upon the dedication of specific individuals. Those who wish to understand the history of the Dharma’s propagation should consult these accounts in detail. In the lineage of the deluded mind, entering the Way does not require seeking it afar; rather, within a single *kṣaṇa* of thought, the three thousand phenomena are manifested.
How could this be the same as the "School Outside the Mountains" (Shanwai), which abandons the deluded to contemplate the true?

Master En, who was initially a lecturer on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, took the "mind-creating" (*xin-zao*) of the *Avataṃsaka* to be the "true mind. From then on, he followed Master Qing of Xianfeng, Master Zhao of Fantian, and Master Yuan of Gushan.
The masters have erroneously maintained a succession of views, all claiming that because one contemplates the true, the meaning is as stated in the *Yishu*:

"It is because from the time of the Master’s own patriarchs and predecessors down to the present, it has been held that the mind alone is the principle (*li*). Such delusion is not unique to the present day;

Because this correct exposition refutes those erroneous discourses, it is said: "It is seen herein," and so forth. Yitang remarked:

"This is the basis upon which the provisional and the real, and the contemplation of the Way, rest within the teachings; thus, Siming’s achievement in reviving the teachings and contemplation lies precisely in this."

To "view the near and see the far" means that by examining the *Zhǐyào* (Essential Points), which is the near, one can perceive the three *bù* (sections), which are the far. To investigate the meaning and intent of the *Zhǐyào* is like dipping one's finger into the cauldron;
only then does one come to know the flavor of the three *bù*. As for "dipping one's finger," it is as stated in the *Zuǒzhuan*: [the story of the man who tasted the meat].
The people of Chu presented a large tortoise to Duke Ling of Zheng (Yi, the crown prince of Duke Mu). The Marquis Song (zi-gong) and Zi-jia (zi-gong was the courtesy name of Song;

zi-jia was the courtesy name of Gui-sheng) were about to present it [to the Duke]. The index finger of Zi-gong twitched, and he showed it to Zi-jia, saying, "If my finger twitches like this on another day, I shall surely taste some extraordinary delicacy.
When they entered, the cook was about to dismember the tortoise; the two looked at each other and laughed. The Duke [heard them].

He questioned him [regarding the reason for his laughter], and Zi-jia informed him. When it came time to eat the large turtles, the Great Officers, he summoned Zi-gong but did not give him any, wishing to prevent the forefinger from providing proof.
Zi-gong was angry; he dipped his finger into the cauldron, tasted the broth, and withdrew.
Now, by taking this slight instance of dipping a finger, one can know the flavor of the entire cauldron, just as by examining two scrolls of a text, one can comprehend the meaning of three sections.

its merit can facilitate understanding for those of the present age who are equally ignorant, and its intent to clarify the provisional and the real within the teachings can resolve the karma of successive generations who collectively mistake the contemplation of the true for the contemplation of the false,
thereby citing the sincere words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs to substantiate these meanings and sever the doubts of scholars.

[Explanation] The answer: Although the errors in the writings of those from outside the mountains do not constitute the orthodox teachings of the Mountain School (Shanjia), they were nonetheless received as studies [from that tradition].

The Tiantai teachings formerly stated that among those who lecture on this school, some demonstrate the *Fengxian* (Offering to the Ancestors) by Master Qing, while others provide commentaries on the *Fahua Wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) and the *Wu'er Men* (Gate of Non-duality) by Master Yu. The *Biography of Ji An* states: "I wish to say 'yún yún'. Master Gu’s commentary explains: "This is equivalent to saying 'thus and so forth' (*rúcǐ rúshì*)."

The *Fuxing* says it signifies that which is not fully expressed; "yún" means speech. The *Shuowen Jiezi* says it represents the appearance of cloud vapors revolving in the sky.

Regarding Shangyou’s words, Master Wenzhong said: "Our ancestor, the Venerable Fazhi, initially relied on Master Qiantang Fengxian Qing’s *Shizhuzhi* (Pointing at the Pearl) commentary on the 'General Summary of the Ten Non-dualities'—specifically the passage stating that all is unified in a single thought-moment—to designate the true mind as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and to separately divide form and mind as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
He further reinterpreted 'transformation' (*zao*), taking it to mean the relationship between essence and function."

This refers to the fact that Master Tiantai Yu, in his commentary on the *Fahua Wenju*, altered twenty-odd characters in the passage concerning the "only contemplation of the inconceivable realm" (*bu er men*)—specifically the text stating "the three thousand [realms] in a single thought are only matter and only mind"—and established it as the meaning of the "True Truth" (*zhen di*).
Master Fazhi took pity on this and rescued the original intent; thus, the *Zhiyao chao* (Essential Commentary) was composed. Therefore, the preface states: "Or..."
Regarding the various indications, notes, and commentaries (the text): the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) on the *Gushan Zhengyi* was composed in the fourth year of the Xiangfu era, after the *Zhiyao*.
As for "phenomena and principle" (*shili*) and so forth, there are many meanings of phenomena and principle as elucidated by this school;

here, it is because those of the Shanwai [school] are confused regarding the phenomena and principle of the three dharmas. The *Yuanlun* (Treatise on the Perfect) states that each of the three dharmas possesses both the two aspects of phenomena and principle.
If one wishes to cultivate the Three Thousandfold World, one must discern that it is not created by a Buddha or a sentient being; rather, one observes only this single thought of deluded mind.

This mind, in its very essence, perfectly possesses the Three Thousandfold World—this is "creation as principle" (*li-zao*). This mind is capable of transformation, creating the Three Thousandfold World—this is "creation as phenomenon" (*shi-zao*).
To understand it in this way is called "wondrous understanding" (*miao-jie*); to contemplate it in this way is called "wondrous practice" (*miao-xing*). Mount [Wu]ai.

The external masters, however, oppose the categories of principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) by means of three dharmas: they claim that mental dharmas belong to principle and are the creator, while the Buddha belongs to phenomena and is the created.
Since the mind belongs to principle, if one points distantly to the True Mind (*zhenxin*), then upon what basis can the initial aspiration open up understanding and establish practice?

Thus we know that as long as the categories of principle and phenomena are not clarified within the Three Dharmas of the Shanwai school, their "wondrous understanding" and "wondrous [practice]" remain unrefined.

Because practice has nothing upon which to rely, Dharma Master Zhong said: "Master Qing further establishes the three thousand [dharmas] of the mental realm as the 'principle-creation' (lizao) and the three thousand [dharmas] of the created Buddhas and sentient beings as the 'phenomenal-creation' (shizao). He is utterly unaware that each of these three categories of dharmas possesses both phenomenal and principle creations.
Therefore, the *Yizhao* refutes this, stating: "Based on his interpretation [extending to] the passage concerning 'non-differentiation,' [Master Qing's view] is forever lost. Thus it is said.

The preface states: "When phenomena and principle are not yet clearly understood, there is no basis for practice or realization. This is all directed at refuting Master Qing. Regarding "Jingxi" and so forth:

Jingxi’s profound interpretation of the Ten Profound Mysteries (*shimiao*) establishes these ten gates, each concluding by returning to the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment" (*yinian sanqian*).

This enables those who cultivate contemplation to easily enter [the truth]. The divergent theories of other masters pointed directly to the True Mind, which conversely caused Jingxi’s [work] to be overlooked.

The subtle understanding has been obscured by the times; our Patriarch, relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, revealed its wondrous purport and established the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle (*yuan-dun zong-cheng*).

He pointed out that all phenomena are perfectly endowed with the three thousand realms of phenomena and principle, intending for sentient beings to open their understanding and establish practice by discerning objects and cultivating contemplation.
Thus, within a single moment of deluded mind, one penetrates the aggregates to realize the inconceivable and manifest the three [mysteries].

If one were to contemplate only the truth among the thousand dharmas while sentient beings remain unawakened to the principle within their phenomenal activities, this would block the gateway for beginners to enter the principle;
if such were the place where contemplation arises, what benefit would the Perfect Teaching of Tiantai have for the capacities of sentient beings?
[Preface] Herein, following the sequence of my lectures, I have composed this *Jiyao chao* (Essential Commentary) at the command of those [disciples].

It is intended to point toward the "infinitesimal mind" as the essential core of phenomena, principle, understanding, and practice. [Explanation] This section clarifies the composition of the work and further explains the meaning of the title.

Regarding the phrase "herein" (*yuan*), it refers to the occasion of lecturing on the *Xuanshi*. As for "following the sequence of lectures," it means that during the course of lecturing on the *Xuanshi*, [the author] addressed the two masters, Qing and Yu.
Regarding the explanation provided below [in the text], some interpret "this single thought-moment" as refuting Master Qing;
others do not accept this and consider it a refutation of Master Yu. This explanatory passage is titled *Zhǐyào chāo* (Essential Notes).

As for the term *ji'ěr* (微細), the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the Practice) states that it means "weak," referring to subtle thoughts. (Text) "With even a minute thought, the three thousand realms are fully present."

The *Enpi* (Commentary on the Perfect Teaching) states that all phenomena are endowed with the three thousand realms (*sanzen*). If one wishes to engage in cultivation, it is necessary to focus on the essential point from the perspective of proximity;
this refers to taking a single thought-moment as the core of both principle and phenomenon. That this mind perfectly possesses the three thousand realms is the essential point of principle;

that the mind can transform and create the three thousand realms is the essential point of phenomenon. As the text says: "Whether phenomenon or principle, both are based upon a single thought-moment."
To provide a general explanation: this single thought-moment possesses two kinds of three-thousandfold worlds. Based on this understanding, one establishes practice;

thus, within the single thought-moment of the mind, one contemplates these three-thousandfold worlds. As the text states: "Both teaching and practice take the contemplation of the mind as their essential point.

It specifically points to the mind because it is the root of all phenomena and the source of all afflictions; for the mind is able to encompass them, and the mind is able to create them. (Jingxi’s *Menmen*).
The conclusion of the Tiantai discourse on the object of contemplation is that its essence resides solely within the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness-aggregate); this is precisely for this reason.

Extending this principle broadly, the entire Great Canon of the Teaching does not transcend this mind; therefore it is said that throughout the course of a lifetime, whether vertically or horizontally, nothing occurs outside of a single thought-moment.
Thus, one should know that the merit of this essential instruction is unsurpassed.

[Commentary] The commentary states: The titles of these texts vary across many editions;

Alternatively, one may place at the beginning the meanings through which [the text] was mastered or the passages by which it was explained; this is done so as not to forget its source.
As for these various supplementary records (*bielu*), their selection and rejection are matters of personal inclination, and there is no need for weary contention.

[Commentary: These ten sections originally appeared in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fmen*). They initially had no titles; later compilers extracted them and each established titles according to their own views.
The title first indicates the three schools: the first belongs to Master Yu, the second to Master Qing, and the third is unknown whose it was established.

Although their formulations differ, they do not transcend two meanings: the first two represent the meaning that is universally applicable, while the third represents the specific text being explained.
Regarding the universally applicable meaning, the ten gates act as the means of penetration (*neng-tong*), and the ten mysteries (*shimiao*) constitute the object of penetration (*suo-tong*).

Regarding the explanation of the text: "Signs" (qiān) refers to that which explains, and "Profound" (xuán) refers to that which is explained. "Not forgetting the source" means one must see that the ten gates emerge from the original text.
Regarding "selection and rejection" and so forth, this indicates the *Zhūzhǐ* (The Pearl-Pointer);

it establishes the title as *Fahua Shimiào Bù'èrmén* (The Ten Profound Non-dual Gates of the Lotus Sutra), and also states that there is a version titled *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Bentì Shimiào Bù'èrmén* (The Profound Dharma Lotus Sutra: Original and Traces, Ten Profound Non-dual Gates).
Regarding the "Gate," some call it the "Gate of the Non-duality of the Original and the Trace of the Lotus Sutra," while others simply refer to it as the "Original and the Trace.
Both of these are later interpolations and are not used here. (Text) In the section on "Question and Answer Resolving Doubts," the titles established by others are extensively refuted;

now, the Master of the *Chao* (Zhiyi) implicitly refutes them, for the titles established by various masters are all private inventions and do not reflect the intention of Jingxi (Zhanran). To adopt them would be improper.
To discard this [view] based solely on human sentiment—why labor so hard to incite contention and extensively refute others by claiming the title of the work is improper?
The Venerable One’s intention was simply to refer to the *Tenfold Non-duality* (*Shimen bu'er men*); thus he stated, "The author established it himself," and cited the subsequent text to explain it.
The *Guishan Zhengyi* (Orthodox Meaning of Mount Gu) states: "The records of the masters were often circulated separately, with their titles marked [independently]."
Regarding the establishment of the title, there are two or three differing opinions from which I shall choose to follow.

Now, relying on Master Xingman’s *Nirvāṇa-ji* (Record of Nirvāṇa), which points toward the *Fahua xuanyi ji shi erbunimen* (The Ten Gates of Non-duality as an Explanatory Record of the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), and considering that Xingman was a disciple of Jingxi [Zhiyi] and must have personally heard his teachings, I have relied upon that record to establish this general title. Although it may contradict the majority, I follow the ancient tradition.

[Text] Although it is said that there is textual evidence [for this], I fear it does not reflect the author’s intention. Among scholars, who does not know that this passage originates from the *Xuánjì* (Profound Record) on the present sutra?
[Commentary] If the four characters "Shí bù'èr mén" (The Ten Non-dual Gates) were established by the author himself, then the text says: "For the sake of those of real capacity... (wéi shíshī).
Provisional teaching (upāya) bifurcates what is non-dual, while the revelation of the Real through provisional means renders duality non-dual.

Since both the Dharma and its pedagogical divisions are thus opened up to form the Sublime, these ten gates take "non-duality" as their heading. One must rely on this text to explain the meaning of the title;

for is it not the case that from the matter and mind discussed throughout the four periods and three teachings, down to those who receive and are moistened by the Dharma, there is nothing that is not distinct and separate?

Therefore, all are termed "two. Now, in this sutra, the ultimate reality is revealed and harmonized; since the ten differences are all integrated, mutually inclusive, and leave nothing outside, they are all termed "non-dual" (*advaya*).

[Commentary] This is the formal explanation of the title. First, it explains "non-dual": the intention behind establishing provisional teachings based on the ultimate reality lies in that reality itself.
Since reality is fundamentally non-dual, yet it is taught as being divided in accordance with the capacities of those following the provisional, it is called "non-dual."

Regarding the intent of the two [aspects of] "opening up the provisional to reveal the real": it lies in the provisional. Since the provisional is of the same essence, not even a hair’s breadth is moved;

thus it is said that they are "two yet non-dual. As for the statement that "the dharmas are equal," Jingxi says: "If one does not rely on the teachings (jiao), one will not know the subtlety of the teachings;

if one does not rely on the sections (bu), one will not know the subtlety of the sections" (text). Since the ten dharmas, beginning with the objective realm (jing), are already established in relation to the teachings...

If one judges according to the provisional divisions and then opens [the teaching], these ten are all wondrous; now, since these ten gates are established based on the ten wonders, they should appropriately be named "Non-duality" (*advaya*).
One must explain them by relying on the wondrous intent of the opening and revealing [of the truth] for them to differ from the "non-duality" of the former sutras.
Is this not precisely the explanation of non-duality that distinguishes between the former and the present teachings by means of duality and non-duality?

If categorized by teaching (*jiao*), the three teachings constitute "two"; if categorized by section (*bu*), the former Perfect [Teaching] that is accompanied by the other vehicles is also not "not-two.
This is because, throughout the four periods, the three teachings have not yet realized the three thousand realms and the three truths as being without differentiation or separation;

therefore, these ten dharmas are all termed "two. In this present sutra, the wondrous principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the three thousand realms is revealed and clarified, and thus the ten dharmas are manifested.
All distinctions are entirely interfused and harmonious: when form is raised, form is subsumed within mind, for there is no phenomenon outside of mind;
the same applies when mind is raised, and even so with sensation and moisture. Therefore, it is said that they mutually subsume one another, leaving nothing external.

[Commentary]: One takes the very substance of non-duality as the gate. Furthermore, it may be said that the ten non-dualities are the means of penetration (*neng-tong*) and the ten wonders (*shih miao*) are the object of penetration (*suo-tong*).

Question: Since the wonders are non-duality and non-duality is the wonders—where both names and substances are identical—how can one distinguish between the means of penetration and the object of penetration?
Answer: Here, we do not distinguish between means and object based on the contrast between the coarse and the wonderful, nor do we base it on the distinction between name and substance.

This is divided because the ten wonderful dharma-characteristics are so vast and comprehensive that they are difficult for scholars to enter. This text extracts the essentials and directly reveals their meaning;

thus, it uses the concise to manifest the extensive, and the easy to penetrate the difficult, establishing the "means of penetration" (*nirukti*) and the "object of penetration. [Commentary] Next, regarding the word "gate" (*mukha*), there are two meanings:
the gate as the essence itself (*svabhāva-mukha*) and the gate as the means of penetration (*nirukti-mukha*). The first phrase refers to the gate as the essence itself; furthermore, below...

One who can penetrate the essential nature itself need not further rely on the distinction between the penetrating subject and the penetrated object; rather, by realizing that they are non-dual in essence, one is able to penetrate and enter.

This is what Mount Guo (Gushan) meant when he said, "Non-duality is itself the gate. This refers to the same principle: the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals and clarifies the wondrous principle of the three thousand realms, which is inherently void and pervasive in its very place.
Because every phenomenon (*dharma*) enters into this state, it serves as the gate; therefore, it is called the "Sūtra of the Essential Nature" (*Dangti Jing*).
"Clouds open the gate of skillful means (upāya-mukha) to reveal the mark of reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa).

Regarding these gates of skillful means and reality, each possesses its own essential nature (*tattva*) that can penetrate both gates. *Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle 8 (24), states: "Reality is non-dual;

because its essential nature is empty and pervasive, it is called a 'gate,' such as the 'Gate of Non-duality' in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* or the 'Dharmadhātu-gate' in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. *Record*, Fascicle 8, states: "Non-obstruction is called [the gate]."
"Emptiness and non-being being unobstructed is called 'penetration' (tong), and thus the entire substance attains the capacity to penetrate; this is the Gate of Penetration. (Text) Four Ming says:

"Outside the gate there is no principle; subject and object are both extinguished. (Text) "Yet they are also equal" means that although all ten gates are each the substance itself, they are established according to their specific meanings;
thus, there is that which penetrates and that which is penetrated. Taking the gate as the penetrator and the wondrous [reality] as the penetrated, it arises.

The question below asks: Generally speaking, that which is said to be "able to penetrate" must take the coarseness of that which is able to penetrate to penetrate the subtlety of that which is penetrated.
Now, non-duality (*advaya*) is itself the subtle, and the subtle is itself non-duality; how can there be a distinction between the subject that penetrates and the object that is penetrated?

Speaking in terms of name and essence: the name is that which is able to penetrate, while the essence is that which is penetrated. Now, both non-duality and the subtle may equally serve as the name, and both may equally serve as the essence.

In the response concerning the division of substance (*tǐ*) into the capable (*néng*) and the object (*suǒ*), the coarse and the subtle (*cūmiào*) are not used to answer the first point above; nor are names and substance used to answer the second point above.
