The fourfold exegesis of the essential phrase "knowing that the contemplation of the mind is the pivot" serves to clarify the sutra. Regarding the first three exegeses, when compared with the subsequent "contemplation of the mind," they all pertain to the realm of phenomena (*vastu*). In the *Myōraku* commentary on the *Shūki*, there are four exegeses:

Exegesis of Causes and Conditions (*hetupratyaya*), Exegesis of the Provisional and the Real (*neyārtha/ nītārtha*), Exegesis of the Original and the Traced (*mūla/anuvyañjana*), and Exegesis of the Contemplation of the Mind.

The meaning of these textual passages is as follows: although the "Original" is remote in time, it is the "Original and Traced"; although the "Provisional and Real" are indeed the Perfect and Sudden, they are the "Provisional and Real"; and although the "Ultimate Truth" is the principle, it is the "Causes and Conditions" (referring here to the mundane within the causal).

The "elements" (dhātu) serve as the antidote to human beings and pertain to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), whereas the "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) pertains to phenomena (*dharma*). (The three explanations regarding the contemplation-mind both pertain to phenomena.

The passage beginning with "others say" below raises false views to criticize the contemplation-mind; it appears that during the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, both the extensive and abbreviated versions of the *Guangming xuanyi* were in circulation, and Master Ciguang En composed a commentary stating: "This work exclusively elucidates the abbreviated version and discards the extensive one."

Regarding the passage on "Contemplating the Mind" (*guanxin*) within the *Benji shifa* (The Ten Dharmas of the Original Text), later generations arbitrarily appended [the section] beginning with Qingzhao;

all subsequent commentators have followed this interpretation, asserting that these ten kinds of threefold dharmas (*shizhong sanshi*) are a discourse on the nature of reality (*faxing*) and do not require the practice of contemplating the mind.

A critique of this view states: "If one were to rigidly discard this text, it would block the gateway for sentient beings to enter into principle and the path leading toward the fruition, leaving them utterly deluded."
Since this is the essential point of the practice and realization of one house (the Tiantai school), it is now said that the harm [caused by misunderstanding] is not slight.

Now, the following questions seek to determine whether a single thought-moment is delusion or awakening. The first two lines establish the premise; from "If already... onwards, the inquiry investigates the matter. Quoting from the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel):
"Sentient beings exist in the realm of phenomena. Since they exist in the realm of phenomena, then a single thought-moment belongs to the delusory; how can it be called true? Nevertheless...
The section "Who Establishes the Analogy of the Vow to Reveal the Gates of Defilement and Purity" states: Although turbidity arises from conditions, turbidity is fundamentally inherent;
this is likened to the defiled mind within delusion. Clarity is likened to the pure mind after fruition, which has never been realized from the outset.
Thus, turbidity is placed first to verify that this mind is illusory. In the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary), it again cites evidence to observe the illusory and reveal the true.

Taking the conscious mind as the object is as stated at the beginning of the fifth fascicle of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary): "Although the preceding section demonstrated the essence [of the object], it merely pointed directly to the mind;
since the mind is the root of all dharmas, the demonstration of the essence was that it is the mind.

Now, therefore, this text uses wondrous contemplation to contemplate it so that it becomes a wondrous object; only then does the object accord with principle. This first section distinguishes and demonstrates the essence of the object.
To take the consciousness of mindfulness as the inconceivable realm is precisely to penetrate the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and realize the inconceivable.
Because one abides in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as previously explained, it is known that what follows demonstrates the intent of contemplating delusion:

although the mind is fundamentally wondrous and its entire substance is pure, when contemplation is not yet perfected, its entire substance is deluded; thus it must be called the delusion of the aggregates. Now, for the purpose of realizing the wondrous, [it is so designated].
Because the Dharma is thus, one uses wondrous contemplation to take its essence as the object; yet if one were to dismiss the lower fetters and denounce them, it would constitute a failure.

Since one has already discarded false contemplation and embraced the true and correct, one now incurs the reproach of "patching the side" (pie-bang) for obstructing [the truth], and further invites the censure of "exclusively relying on the principle-nature for wondrous bliss" while breaking down the nine realms.

Furthermore, as for the following, both the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) and the present text observe the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) to examine and refute [delusions].

Question: One now wishes to contemplate the mind—does the present momentary deluded aggregate (*skandha*) already possess the three thousand [realms], or must one first realize the true principle for them to be possessed?
If the true is revealed within the deluded, then by taking this conscious mind as the wondrous [nature], why is it necessary to establish a separate "true mind"?
Furthermore, Tiantai taught that in *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, he personally instructed practitioners to contemplate the present aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*).

Furthermore, in all nine objects below those that have been raised, as well as in each section on the four foundations of mindfulness, it is stated that one contemplates the single thought-moment of ignorance (*avidyā-citta*).

How can you so stubbornly contradict the teachings of the school and establish a "True Mind" separately? I suspect that when the Patriarch established names such as the "five aggregates," he was merely providing a provisional designation for the methods of practice;
it was not intended as a definitive [ontological] position, yet you have established it as such yourself. Moreover, the phrase "if it were equal" and so forth is intended as a precaution.

If one were to further argue that the "single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*) mentioned here is not the same as the objects of meditation such as the "aggregates" (*skandha*) in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, yet it still cannot be restated through the ten gates so that the practice of contemplation may be recognized—then the general principle of the contemplative method would be established with correct understanding as its primary focus and cessation (*śamatha*) as secondary, rendering the phrase "identical to the essence of contemplation" entirely superfluous. Furthermore, regarding the term "middle": [it refers to] using another...

Regarding the establishment of a thesis and the subsequent refutation by another: they claim that while principle (*li*) is universal and phenomena (*shi*) are particular, now that one distinguishes them separately—such as within the categories of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*)—the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is a single reality whose essence is solely principle, yet it is specifically attributed to the mind. Now we ask:

within this distinction, how does the "true mind" (*zhēn xīn*) differ from the "universal true mind"? If you say they are different, both are the true mind; if you say they are the same, [how can there be a distinction?]

If the general and the particular are not distinguished, how much less can they be separately assigned? To claim that the "particular" belongs to the mind is precisely correct according to principle; what, then, does "principle" mean if there is no distinction within it?

[Commentary] The two characters for "mind-nature" (xìngxīng) are not different, yet they are distinct. Since it is said that "the unchanging follows conditions" (*bùbiàn suíyuán*), that which is named "mind" is precisely the principle.

To follow conditions without changing is called "nature" (*xing*); this is the principle that nature is identical to phenomena. Now, because one wishes to manifest the principle within phenomena, both are cited together.
Following this pattern, it should be said: "following conditions without changing is called Buddha," and "following conditions without changing is called nature.
It should be understood that birth and nature are likewise so; all three dharmas are equally phenomena and equally principles, differing from other interpretations of the mind.

Thus, to interpret the principle as being universal for both Buddhas and sentient beings, while interpreting phenomena as being distinct, is the interpretation of other schools regarding the meaning of "mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.
This does not deeply penetrate the fundamental teaching; by indiscriminately employing the tenets of other traditions, it causes much harm. Where, then, lies its true intent?

[Commentary] Regarding the two characters "mind-nature" (*xin-xing*), they encompass both delusion and enlightenment. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the "ever-abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature" pertains to enlightenment.
The *Yi-shu* (Treatise on Meaning) states that it is exclusively the nature of the single thought-moment of the *ālaya*-consciousness of ordinary beings;
this pertains to delusion. Now, it is said that while the mind-nature is not different, the phenomena are different, for principle and phenomena are mutually identical.
Therefore, while "nature" (xing) belongs to the principle of non-alteration, "mind" (xin) is the phenomenon that follows conditions and thus differs.

The general meaning is this: "non-altering while following conditions" is called mind; this is the phenomenon that is identical to the principle. "Following conditions while not altering" is called nature;
this is the principle that is identical to the phenomenon. This passage cites both together because it seeks to reveal the principle by means of the phenomenon. Next, with this...

The mind follows the same principle as that [of the Buddha and sentient beings]: both the Buddha and sentient beings are the unchanging following conditions (*avikāra-anu-pratyaya*), and both are the phenomena (*dharma*) that are identical to the principle (*li*).
Furthermore, since they are both called "Buddha" and "sentient being" through the unchanging following conditions, it is said that they are likewise so.

One should know that what this school discusses regarding the mind, Buddha, and sentient beings is that their phenomena are all phenomena and their principles are all principles; they are not the same as others. This concludes the refutation of the [Mount] Shan [school].

Externally, [some] have indiscriminately employed the *Huayan Dashu* (Great Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra) of other schools, taking the mind-nature (*cittaprakṛti*) as the principle (*li*) and the creator, and asserting that Buddhas and sentient beings are the created.
This is how other schools interpret the meaning of the non-differentiation of the three—Buddha, mind, and sentient beings.

Because the compassionate light of the Tiantai teachings does not deeply penetrate this, when lecturing on the Huayan Sutra alongside the Tiantai teachings, they indiscriminately employ this interpretation, thereby obstructing our own school.
The three dharmas each possess the principle of the twofold creation of phenomena and reality.

[Commentary] Regarding "the nature is one," etc.: although the nature is one, because there is no fixed nature of oneness, the three thousand phenomena of form and mind appear with their characteristics distinct and vivid.
One should know that this is the establishment of all dharmas from the groundless root. If...
Since this principle applies to both reality (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), the seventh record explains this passage as follows:

"Reality is the nature-virtue (*xingde*); phenomena are the cultivation-virtue (*xiude*). When deluded, they flow as the three paths; when awakened, they constitute the supreme functions within the fruit.
These four layers are all established based on the true aspect (*shixiang*) within delusion. Now, the commentary states: "Within delusion, the true..."
The mutual identity [of phenomena] is the root of non-abiding; this is precisely what is meant here by "the single nature being without nature.
The aforementioned four layers establish all dharmas; this is precisely what is meant here by the "three thousand [realms] being manifest.
Since the first layer takes the inherent merit of the conditions and the response as all dharmas, it must take the true cause as the root of non-abiding. As for the remaining three layers, since...
The two modes of cultivation—contrary and conforming—are for all phenomena necessarily based upon the three causes of inherent virtue as their root of non-abiding;

this constitutes the general and specific aspects of both principle and phenomena. Question: Since the true reality within delusion is taken as the "one nature" in contrast to the "three thousand" as the "specific," it is precisely appropriate to take principle as the general; why then do you labor to refute others? Answer: Because of the three thousand phenomena...
Because they are of one identical nature, when following conditions to manifest as the myriad phenomena, taking up a single phenomenon serves to encompass all.

Since sentient beings have been entirely immersed in delusion from time immemorial, if one were to discuss only the true nature as the universal, how could it fully encompass every particular phenomenon?
Therefore, one specifically takes up a single thought-moment; this is established as the object of contemplative wisdom based on what is proximate and essential.
Furthermore, if one demonstrates that a single thought-moment (ekakṣaṇa) universally encompasses all phenomena, it reveals that all phenomena share the same true nature.
Thus, the *Shiqian* states: "The conventional consists of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses; the true resides together within a single thought-moment.

One must know that only by sharing the same nature can they coexist within a single thought-moment. Therefore, the coexistence within a single thought-moment is used to manifest the identity of the single true nature.

It does not mean that a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is immediately designated as the True Reality (*satyadharma*); how could it be that sharing a single particle (*paramāṇu*) is not the True Reality?
In this passage, "one nature" (*eka-dhātu*) serves as the general principle, while in the preceding and following passages, "one thought-moment" serves as the general principle;
this is because principle and phenomena manifest one another. These two phrases precisely set forth the reason for subsuming the particular into the general. This is by virtue of the one nature.
Because Wuxing established the three thousand [realms] based on both principle and phenomena, these two layers of three thousand reside together within a single thought-moment.

How could this be the same as other interpretations that directly designate "a single thought-moment" as the true nature (*tathatā*)? [Commentary: Regarding the explanation of the latter two phrases, the initial passage—beginning with "Although the nature...

and ending with "is manifest"—is the correct interpretation of "one nature. This "nature" refers to the essence of nature itself; the absence of a fixed nature is precisely what constitutes the delusion of nature.

Regarding this nature: because there are two aspects to this nature—true permanence and unchangingness versus following conditions and being defiled by habituation—the former refers to the "one nature that does not change," which is the nature [itself], while the latter refers to "the absence of nature," which is the nature of defiled habituation.

This means that although the essence of this nature is the single principle of true permanence, its character is fused and subtle, and is not fixed; it is also the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*), lacking any solid substance.
Because it abides in its nature, this wondrous nature is fully endowed with the three thousand [realms]. Next, these are identical to the fundamental dharma;

in this text, the single nature and the absence of nature are themselves the foundation of non-abiding, wherein the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest. This refers to the established dharmas. One should know that both principle and phenomena each possess their own fundamental dharma;
therefore, it is said that "all have" [them]. This cites the four phrases from the commentary on the seventh [chapter] regarding the causes for establishing the dharmas.

The *Shu* (Commentary) explains the scripture’s statement regarding "one mark and one flavor" as follows: "One mark" refers to the ground of non-abiding (*wuzhu ben*) from which all phenomena are established;

"non-abiding and markless" means there is no differentiation, while "establishing all phenomena" means there is differentiation. The *Ji* (Sub-commentary) explains: "One mark is the ground of non-abiding that establishes all phenomena.
In principle, this is the nature-virtue (*xingde*); in fact, it is the object of conditions (*yuanli*). In principle, it is the inherent virtue; in fact, it is cultivation (*xiu*)."
The three virtues (guṇas), the three causes (hetus), and so forth—these four phrases constitute two layers of established principles (*dharmasthāpana*).

The first layer states: "In principle, there are the nature-virtues of the conditions and the understanding (*pratyaya* and *bodhi*). (The nature-virtues of the cause are the primary cause; the nature-virtues of the conditions and understanding are the established phenomena. "In fact, there are the practice-virtues of the three causes" (which follow the direction of cultivation).

"In delusion, one flows through the three paths" (which represent reverse cultivation). "In awakening, there are the superior functions of the fruit" (which also belong to forward cultivation; since one must transform others from cause to fruit, they are called "superior functions").

Next, the three layers are all based on the three causes of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) as the "root of non-abiding" (*amūla-sthiti*). The establishment of the four propositions is as detailed below in the commentary on the *Sutra*.

Regarding the phrase "now explaining," this refers to a harmonious interpretation of the current text. It states that all four layers arise from delusion regarding the true reality (*bhūta-tathatā*), thereby establishing the root of non-abiding;
furthermore, while the first three layers can be understood through delusion, the fourth layer—the function of the fruit—likewise proceeds from it.

Miyasaka says: Because the fruit is achieved through the cause, it is also achieved through delusion regarding principle; thus, at the stage of fruition, the principle and phenomena are integrated, both being rooted in principle.

These four levels do not transcend the three thousand [realms] of principle and phenomena, each having its own fundamental dharma. Since practice has both the inverse and the direct, and the cause must necessarily achieve the fruit, there are these four levels.
This is the "convergence of the same activity" (dōji) at the lower level, wherein the principles of the general and the particular are unified.
In the first [case], one takes the three causes of the inherent nature (*prakṛti*) as the fundamental basis, which is the general principle;

the conditions and results (*pratyaya-phala*) of the inherent qualities of nature are the established phenomena, which is the specific principle. Next, one takes the three causes of the inherent qualities of nature as the fundamental basis, which is the general phenomenon;

the two types of cultivation—contrary and conforming—are the established phenomena, which is the specific phenomenon. Now, I ask: since the subsequent [section] again speaks of "inherent qualities of nature," why are they termed "phenomena"?

Since it is said that there are three causes, how can one speak of a comprehensive answer? Although it is said that the entirety of the nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) resides within delusion, and although these three causes are but the single reality-mark (*dharmatā*), it is therefore stated that they all arise from the reality-mark within delusion.

If this is so, then the primary cause (*hetu*) of the first stage is also the reality-mark within delusion; why then do you say the principle provides a comprehensive answer? It is precisely because whether it be phenomena (*dharma*) or...

In principle, all [teachings] take the contemplation of phenomena as their totality; thus, the meaning is perfectly consistent. In the question and answer, the selection between phenomena and principle is first made based on the nature being fundamentally identical to the principle as the totality.

Since the inquiry has already used the fundamental dharma to provide an exegesis for the present text—wherein the true reality within delusion is precisely this "one nature" and "naturelessness"—then "one nature" is the totality and the "three thousand" are the particulars. Since the one nature...
This is the actual reality, the correct principle, which provides a general answer: that the nature of all dharmas is identical and thus may be taken collectively as a whole.
Now, in order to establish contemplation, we point to the mind as the essential core; for the three thousand realms of form and mind share the same true, eternal, and unchanging nature.

Since these phenomena are entirely transformations of this unchanging nature according to conditions (*pratyaya*), and since all phenomena are of one and the same nature, it suffices to take up any single instance.
To summarize all dharmas under a single principle: since all sentient beings from the very beginning have never been separated from thought, one must point directly to the point of delusion.
If one were to take ultimate truth as the summary, how could all dharmas be mutually inclusive? Therefore, we now specifically designate "a single thought" (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*).
Among all dharmas, this is selected because it is proximate; furthermore, it is established as the object of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-viṣaya*). Once this single [thought] is known...
When "mindfulness" (*nian*) is taken as the comprehensive totality, it clearly reveals that they share the same true nature; for it is precisely within delusion that the true manifests.

Therefore, the *Sub-commentary* (*Qiwen*) is cited to authenticate this present "single thought-moment" as the totality. That text, in explaining the seven and two realms of the Two Truths, first adopts a trans-segmental approach with the intent of showing things in brief, stating:
"Only the dharma-nature is pointed out as the True Truth (*satyadharma*), while ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination [are the conventional truth]."
Regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), its meaning is already sufficient; the *Shiqianshi* (Explanatory Notes) states: "There is only the single dharma-nature.

When contrasted with ignorance, it reaches the point that while the two truths—conventional as the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses—are distinct, the real (*paramārtha*) is co-resident within a single thought-moment (text).

The meaning of the present passage is that the "hundred realms and thousand suchnesses" are precisely the "three thousand [realms] as they are" (*yǎnrán*) mentioned in the current text; they are identical.
To abide in a single thought-moment is precisely what is meant here by "one nature having no nature. This merit arises because all phenomena are identical to the single true nature;
thus, they are able to coexist within the totality of a single thought-moment. Now, by using phenomena to reveal principle, delusion is penetrated and transformed into reality;

therefore, the function of a single thought-moment is used to manifest the single true reality. How could those outside the [Tiantai] school possibly interpret this as "true principle"? One must know that this is the perfect expression of all things.

The mutual inclusion and mutual possession of the dharmas are now specifically pointed toward the mind for the purpose of establishing contemplation; thus, it is said they "dwell together within a single thought-moment.

If they dwell together within a single sense-object (*dhātu*), would that not be the Truth? The concluding indication at the end of this passage clarifies the meaning of the preceding and following points.

The previous statement says they are "all in one thought-moment," while the subsequent statement asks, "How could they deviate from one thought-moment? This refers to the preceding and following texts as being of a single nature.
Because principle (*li*) is the principle within the particular when one moment of thought (*yi-nian*) points to a phenomenon, it is said that "one nature is the principle";

because phenomena are the manifestations of this nature, it is said that "one moment of thought is the manifestation. These two lines—"this one nature is without nature" and "the three thousand [worlds] are perfectly present"—precisely clarify the reason why, by establishing the particular based on the universal, the particular is able to be subsumed into the universal. This is the basis of non-abiding. All... [text ends].

The origins of the Mahāyāna sūtras are not of a single source, yet none manifest their meaning more clearly than the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, specifically in the middle volume, the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings.
There, Mañjuśrī asks Vimalakīrti: "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome? He replies:

"The body is the root" (referring to the *sarvatra-gata-bhūmi*). Again he asks: "What is the root of the body? He replies: "Desire and greed are the root" (referring to the *kāmarāga-bhūmi*). Furthermore...
Question: What is the root of sensual desire? Answer: False conceptualization is its root (the ground of abiding in the craving for form).
Question again: What is the root of false conceptualization? Answer: Perverted perception is its root (the ground of abiding in the craving for the formless).
Question again: What is the root of perverted perception? Answer: Non-abiding is its root (the ground of abiding in ignorance). Question again: What is the root of non-abiding?
The original answer states: "Because there is no abiding, there is no root. Mañjuśrī established all dharmas from the root of non-abiding (text).
In the seventh fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha says to Ānanda: "Based on this non-abiding, he establishes the world and all sentient beings" (text).

Furthermore, the Great Master [Zhiyi] did not fail to see that in the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there is but a single characteristic and a single flavor.
Regarding its meaning: first, Tiantai cites it as in the *Miaoxuan*, clarifying the fundamental and the trace through principle and phenomena;

second, as in the *Wenju* commentary on the sutra, explaining the single characteristic and single flavor; third, as in the *Wenju* commentary on the "Expedient Means" chapter, explaining the ten pairs of provisional and real;
fourth, first regarding principle and phenomena, as in the *Guangmingxuan*, the two sequences of arising—contrary and conforming—from the non-abiding foundation.
The *Yi* (義) [of Zhiyi] states in the *Siming* (四明): "Regarding the meaning of 'lacking firm abiding,' the *Sheshi* (捨遺記) explains it as follows:

'It is entirely because the secret nature of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) is the nature of lacking firm abiding; therefore, the Great Sage takes this non-abiding nature of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) as the foundation.

(Text). Furthermore, the *Bixing Xuanyi* (別行玄記), Part II, states: "Because the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) is fundamentally free from abiding and attachment, it is the foundation of non-abiding."
The *Zhijyao* states: "Although the nature is one, it lacks a fixed nature of oneness. (Text) The *Jingjue yibian* states:
Some say that "the basis of non-abiding" means that the nature does not abide determinately. True Suchness is neither quiescent nor illuminating, yet it is both quiescent and illuminating;
this is the nature's lack of determinate abiding. That the essence of ignorance is empty while establishing all phenomena is likewise the nature.

The claim that there is no basis for this interpretation—that [the mind] does not abide [in ignorance]—is likely due to not having consulted the original commentary (*śāstra*). The commentary explains "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*) by stating that there is no fundamental source (*mūla*):

it says that ignorance (*avidyā*) relies upon the *dharmatā*, and that the *dharmatā* is none other than ignorance; since these two are non-dual and without distinction, how could the *dharmatā* itself rely upon the *dharmatā*?
One should know, therefore, that ignorance has no fundamental source. Furthermore, the commentary explains the meaning of "non-abiding" as being "beginningless" (*anādi*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) arises because afflictions such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) all have a basis upon which they arise;
since their arising has a beginning, this [ignorance] arises without a basis and thus has no beginning. Therefore, it is called "beginningless ignorance.
This very point clarifies that "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*) means "without basis. How could it ever mean that the nature [of things] does not abide? (Text: Refuting the Four)
The *Mingwu ju* (Clarifying the Lack of Basis) relies solely on its own commentary to establish the meaning of "lack of basis" (*wuyi*).

Now, I say that while the commentary explains the sūtra’s "non-abiding" (*wuzhu*) by means of the meaning of "lack of basis," how can it be mistakenly cited here to explain the "basis of non-abiding" (*wuzhuben*)?
The fourth section, "The Meaning of Lacking Firm Abiding," profoundly captures the intent of Jingxi’s text. As the *Miaole* states: "This basis of non-abiding is fully explained as follows."
The seventh fascicle of the *Zhuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) explains: "Dharmatā is itself ignorance; dharmatā has no place of abiding. Ignorance is itself dharmatā;
ignorance has no place of abiding. Although both ignorance and dharmatā have no place of abiding, they act as the root for all phenomena.
The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) states: "Non-abiding is the name for the 'root'; non-abiding is the root" (*wuzhu jiben*, *wuzhuben*). Next, [the text] distinguishes [these].
Regarding the "Exegesis on the *Wondrous Joy of Establishing Dharmas through the Four Phrases*," it states: "The first aspect is that the root of non-abiding establishes all dharmas.
As for principle, it is the nature-virtue; as for phenomena, it is the practice-virtue. When deluded, these three causes flow through the three paths;
when awakened, they become the supreme functions within the fruit. These four layers are all established by means of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) within delusion" (text).

Jingxi established these four propositions precisely to capture the original intent of the sutra and its commentary. The "Dharmatā as the fundamental nature" refers to what the sutra calls "the single mark up to the mark of quiescence," which the commentary explains as:
"The mind-nature of sentient beings is itself the liberation of inherent virtue (xingde), far removed from the three marks [of birth, abiding, and extinction], and is quiescent.

The "three causes of cultivated virtue" (xiude) refers to what the sutra calls "the single flavor," which the commentary explains as follows: [The three causes of cultivation are the causes of the path, the cause of the fruit, and the cause of the Dharma-body].
It is said that when the Tathāgata speaks these three dharmas with a single voice, they are themselves the three samādhis;
these three characteristics constitute the practice of the Middle Way as the conditionally arisen object. The Record states: "Because the Buddha has spoken, this nature can be cultivated.
This again points to the three natures as the objects of cultivation. Regarding the flow of the three paths, the Commentary states: "The nature-virtue is simply that which is originally possessed."
The characteristic of liberation from the three paths is the virtue of liberation from the path of karma; the characteristic of detachment is the virtue of *prajñā* from the path of afflictions;
and the characteristic of quiescence is the virtue of the *dharmakāya* from the path of suffering.
The supreme function within the fruit is what the Sūtra calls "ultimately reaching all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*), while the Commentary states that "in the end, one becomes the One."

The *Commentary on the Scripture of the Fruit of All-Knowledge* merely states that one realizes the fruit through self-cultivation; since there is self-realization, there must subsequently follow the transformation of others, hence it speaks of "superior function.
This also accords with the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanquan jiaozhi*). The first emphasis is to manifest that the nature-merits (*xingde*) are inherently complete;

thus, the direct cause (*zhengyin*) is taken as the basis, while the conditional and responsive causes (*yuanliang*) are established as the phenomena. That is, the principle-inherently-contained three thousand realms (*lishu sanqian*) is primary. The second emphasis is for... [text continues].

This clarifies that cultivation arises from the perfection of nature; thus, the three aspects of nature serve as the foundation, while the three aspects of cultivation serve as the established phenomena.

This means that the entire body [of reality] gives rise to its function, manifesting and creating the three thousand realms. The *Yiyao* cites this to harmonize and explain how "the one nature is without nature, yet the three thousand realms are perfectly present.
This is because other teachers point to the mind as the principle, whereas for [this school], both Buddhas and sentient beings are the phenomena themselves, which are exclusively the principle.

Since the "total phenomena" (*sāmānya-dharma*) are merely specific instances, [the text] specifically cites that both the cultivated and the inherent have their own fundamental dharmas, thereby manifesting that both phenomena and principle possess both the general and the particular.
Furthermore, Siming directly employs two layers [of analysis], as it says:
"In the first layer, since the inherent *pratyaya* and *jñāna* are taken as the dharmas to be established, one must take the 'correct cause' as the basis of non-abiding; as for the remainder..."

The three layers [of the *Wujinzhu*] take the two practices of "contrary" and "conformable" as the established teachings; these must necessarily have the three causes of inherent virtue (*xingde*) as their fundamental basis for non-abiding (text).

The first layer concerns the three dharmas within the nature itself (*xingzhong sanfa*) in their own right; the second layer concerns the relative relationship between practice and nature (*xiuxing xiangdui*).
Regarding the pure awakening, the *Bujia bian* states: "In recent times, those who uphold the treatises mostly follow their own arbitrary whims, resulting in errors regarding 'non-abiding'."
To establish dharmas based on a single nature is an error; thus, the fundamental and the derivative become entangled, and the source and the flow are conflated.
Furthermore, it is said that while the first [of the four] may be so, the remaining three are not. This implies that the other three stages are the three gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha).

Since the three causes of cultivated virtue (bhāvanā-guṇa) have already been established as the dharmas to be realized, one must necessarily take the three causes of innate virtue (prakṛti-guṇa) as their respective counterparts.
The Master replied: "To claim that non-abiding is the root is to fail to understand the principle of the union and separation of cultivation and nature (*xing*). Why is this?

Although, in terms of nature, one is separated from conditions, in cultivation one must unite with them. Because within nature the *niṣyanda-hetu* (revealing cause) has never yet initiated the aspiration for enlightenment, and the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause) has never yet applied its practice, they are both designated as the *samyak-hetu* (correct cause).
Within correct cultivation, the *samyak-hetu* is that which is illuminated by the *niṣyanda-hetu* and that which is activated by the *pratyaya-hetu*."

"Strictness" (or "rigor") is simply the foundation of non-abiding. The *Ji* (Record) states: "In terms of phenomena, the three causes for cultivating virtue are presented alongside the fundamental [nature].
This is, for example, like when Zhiyi, in his commentary on the *Wuliangyi jing*, explains that from the one dharma four fruits arise;

Jingxi says: "The Perfect Buddha is the 'one,' while the three provisional [teachings] arise from it; because the subject and object are relative, they are called the 'four Buddhas. Now, it is also like this.

It is precisely because the fundamental (xing) gives rise to the conditional (yuan), and the cultivated (xiu) and the nature (xing) stand in relation to one another, that they are called the "three causes.
Furthermore, the *Xiuxing-buxing-erbu-men* states: "Although the cultivated is seen as nine, the nine are merely three examples; now, although the cultivated possesses three, the three are but one.
Master Jingjue’s intention was that the "non-abiding" (wuzhu) is but the single nature (xing); while phenomena (fa) are established, they can only be so.

Second, regarding the cultivation: if one were to judge the remaining three layers by taking the three natures as the basis, this would mean that the two cultivations are conflated with a single nature (hence it is said:

"the lack of nature in cultivation differs from the single nature"). If one takes the three cultivations as the established dharma, this means that a single nature is erroneously confused with the two cultivations (hence it is said:

"the establishment of dharmas is erroneous regarding the two cultivations"). Because the differences in cultivation are used as the dharma, the derivative confuses the fundamental; because the nature is erroneously identified with cultivation, [the fundamental is lost].

The root is confused with the branches (hence it is said that "the root and branches are mutually confused"). Now, it is said that the establishment of the four grave offenses is Master Jingxi’s original intent for his commentary on the sutra;
since he takes the three causes and the three paths as the dharmas to be established, he must take the three natures (*xing-san*) as the basis of non-abiding.

If one refutes the Four Ming [School], one is refuting Master Jingxi. Regarding the nature, there is constant opening; only when contrasted with cultivation does it become "conformity. This is the case.

The nature-seed (*prakṛti-bīja*) consists of the three paths and their adversaries; the three virtues (*guṇa*) correspond to and counteract them. When the categories of the seed-nature are combined with the nature itself, these three become one.

This refers to the meaning of the mutual relationship between the cultivated (*bhāvanā*) and the innate (*prakṛti*). As for the current text, it concerns the meaning of the respective three dharmic characteristics of the cultivated and the innate, and their mutual correspondence.

How could you recklessly refute this? Does Zhiyi [Sì-míng] not understand the separation and combination of the cultivated and the innate? Furthermore, if you claim that the three causes of cultivated virtue—

Regarding this simultaneous presentation of both [the nature and the cultivation], should the three paths of transmigration also be understood in this way? The positions established by Xuanzang (Xingju) are all untenable.

Within the Perfect and Real Teaching (*yuanshi jiao*), the dharma-substance of both cultivation and nature each possesses the three factors; it has never been heard that nature consists only of the direct cause (*zhengyin*) while cultivation consists only of the conditional and responsive causes (*yuan* and *liao*).
To advance, it does not constitute the Perfect [Teaching]; to retreat, it does not constitute the Separate [Teaching]. Examine the *Guanming* [Sutra].

The ten kinds of threefold dharmas in the *Xuan* (Profound) [treatise] present two sequences of arising: the first concerns the sequence of inverted arising, which infers the principles of the teaching from the phenomena to reveal that they arise through inversion;
the second concerns the sequence of direct arising, which establishes practice and cultivation to turn back from delusion toward reality.
The first [of these two] establishes all teachings from the non-abiding source of the dharma-nature; the second [establishes them] from the non-abiding of ignorance.
The fundamental establishment of all dharmas of practice is synthesized through four propositions. The *Shiyiji* states:
"The present first section corresponds to the superior function within that fourth fruit; the present second section corresponds to the three causes for cultivating virtue within that second [fruit].
Jingjue (Wen) asserts that among the ten kinds of triple dharmas, the Buddha-nature of the three causes refers precisely to the first two propositions.

The true cause of Buddha-nature inherently possesses the two cultivations, which are identical to its intrinsic virtue (*xingde*); the two cultivations of conditions and fulfillment (*yuanliao*) together give rise to this single nature, which is identical to its cultivated virtue (*xiude*).
Thus, the three causes arise in both reverse and direct orders, corresponding to the second and third lines [of the verse].

Taking ignorance as the basis, ten kinds of triple dharmas are established, which constitute the phrases on the cyclic flow of the three paths. Taking the Dharma-nature as the basis, [ten kinds of triple dharmas are likewise established].
The ten sets of three dharmas constitute the phrases regarding the supreme functions within the fruit.

If one interprets the fundamental dharma in this manner, how can it be that among these ten sets, only three causes are specifically selected for analysis and correlated with the first two phrases, while the remaining nine sets are not?
Second, from the non-abiding of ignorance, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are established; thus they are established.
The practice of cultivation follows the sequence of arising; why, then, is it called the "threefold flow of transmigration"? To synthesize these two layers of general and specific essentials:
in the first layer, the inherent qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*) of the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature serve as the established dharma, which must take the correct cause (*samyag-hetu*) as its basis.

In the remaining three layers, the two types of cultivation—contrary and conforming—serve as the established dharma, which must necessarily take the three aspects of the inherent nature as their basis.
This refers to the two levels of totality and particularity regarding both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). (Text) An old question asks:
"If the bases of the two levels both belong to principle, and the totalities of the two levels both reside in phenomena;

furthermore, if the basis of the second level is the threefold Dharma-nature, while the totalities of the two levels are both the single thought-moment—since phenomena and principle differ, and the 'one' and 'three' are distinct, how can they be reconciled as the same?"
Beifeng says: The two layers of "general and particular" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) are established based on phenomena; thus, both take the single thought-moment as the general.
The two layers of the fundamental dharma are established by tracing back their merit; thus, both take the principle-nature (*li-xing*) as the foundation. Why is this?

Because both layers of general and particular arise from the single nature, they can be subsumed generally within a single thought-moment. Regarding phenomena, this occurs within delusion; regarding things, one takes the thing itself as the general, thereby tracing back its merit.

The nature of "returning" (*guixing*) may also take principle (*li*) as its totality; thus, Siming said: "In this text, the single nature is taken as the totality, so that phenomena (*shi*) and principle manifest one another.

Although these two layers of establishing the dharma both trace their merit back to principle, taking principle as the foundation, since the true reality (*shixiang*) exists even within delusion, one should know that with respect to the dharmas themselves, phenomena may also be taken as the foundation. As for such...

This means that when one traces back the function from both the general and the specific, it is equal to the fundamental dharma; and when the fundamental dharma is present in phenomena, it is equal to the general and the specific.
The *Wenjingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) states: "The nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is identical to ignorance; they are non-dual and without distinction.

One should know that ignorance has no root. The *Jian* (Sub-commentary) states: "The nature of dharmas is identical to ignorance, yet the nature of dharmas takes ignorance as its root" (text). This is purity.
Question: Since they are identical, there is no fundamental basis (*mūla*). Why does the *Shuqiǎn* (Explanatory Notes) say that because they are identical, it serves as the basis? Answer:

The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) explains that when there is no abiding, there is no basis; the *Shuqiǎn* explains the "basis of non-abiding. Therefore, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and ignorance are mutually identical, and each may serve as the basis for the other.
Question: The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), after establishing the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), states: "It is fully as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Shuqiǎn*. [End of excerpt]

Question: Since the commentary states that there is no establishment of the four propositions, why do you point to them so vaguely? Answer: This specifically points to the meaning of the "basis of non-abiding" (*amūla*) in the commentary;
it does not refer to the establishment of the four propositions.
△ Second, from "One should know" onwards, the truth-objects are clarified through principle and phenomena. Part one: Clarifying the three truths by means of principle and phenomena.

Second, first clarifying principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). One should know that the form and mind of the mind are precisely the mind; "transformation" (*bian*) is the name for this, and "creation" (*zao*) is its designation. "Creation" refers to essence and function. [Commentary:

Regarding the great outline of clarifying the realm of truth (*di-jing*) by way of principle and phenomena: previously, the general and specific were explained without yet distinguishing between principle and phenomena; now, phenomena are clarified.

Regarding the principle that possesses both the general and the particular: first, in clarifying the three truths by means of principle and phenomena (*dharma*), since both the inherent presence of principle (*li-jù*) and the phenomenal manifestation (*shi-zào*) are empty, provisional, and the Middle, one first clarifies principle and phenomena, followed by the summary of the three truths. First, as for "mind," this refers to the mind capable of possessing [all things] in each moment;
this is the generality of principle. As for "form and mind," these refer to the three thousand [realms] possessed [by them]; this is the particularity of principle. This is...

"Mind" refers to the totality of the three thousand [realms] within the mental events of a single *kṣaṇa* mentioned above; "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the individuality of the three thousand phenomena produced by those events.
As for naming "transformation" as "production" (*nirmāṇa*), this transformation is also called production because it transforms and produces in accordance with conditions;

it is not a matter of artificial construction. This constitutes the two levels of totality and individuality regarding both phenomena and principle; such is this process of transformation and production.
Since it is the function of the entire substance, it is said that "creation" refers to substance and function.
[Commentary] "The mind and its form-and-mind" clarify that principle is inherent within phenomena. The initial mention of "mind" serves to point toward a single moment (*kṣaṇa*);
the particle "zhi" is a grammatical filler. "Form-and-mind" refers to the three thousand virtues of the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*). This is how the Perfect Teaching elucidates nature.

It is not merely principle alone, but rather possesses the nature of the three thousand [realms]. This nature is perfectly interfused and universally penetrates the momentary mind within the realm of shared residence (*sahā-loka*).

The matter and mind of this mind are simply the mind itself as the three thousand; these three thousand aspects of matter and mind, like the eight phases of a material object, possess no sequence of before or after.
This is identical to the meaning of the "mind-inclusion" (*citta-samgraha*) in *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, which likewise points toward the nature of the mind.
The meaning of this is that the three thousand [dharmas] of form and mind cannot be altered by even one iota; therefore, they are called "nature" (*xing*).

This single phrase clarifies the general and the particular as being fundamentally complete from the perspective of principle (*li*). The three thousand [dharmas] are the particular, while a single moment of thought is the general.

Because the three thousand share the same nature, the general is contained within a single moment of thought. [Commentary: First, the direct explanation; second, the analytical examination (*liaojian*). The first part further consists of three sections.

The first section explains the first phrase, which is the ultimate mindfulness of the mind that is inherently endowed with both the general and the specific. The first phrase cites the text to clarify the inherent presence of the general through the particular;

it specifically indicates the term "mind" (citta) and indicates that "matter-and-mind" (rūpa-citta) is inherently endowed with principle. Regarding the phrase "First, below," this explains [the nature];

regarding the phrase "In the *Yuanlun*," this sets forth the intent: the *Yuanlun* teaches that the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is not the principle of the "inherent presence of phenomena" found in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) or the Distinct Teaching (*vyatireka-śāsana*).

The nature is perfectly interfused and universally pervasive: there is not a single dharma that is partial, which is called "perfect" (yuan); there is not a single dharma that is distinct, which is called "interfused" (rong).

Every dharma is all-pervasive and every dharma mutually enters one another, solely because the essential substance of the nature of all dharmas is perfectly interfused, mutually pervasive, and mutually entering, even within a single moment of existence.
This mind is utterly devoid of subject and object below, while above it clearly manifests both form and mind.

All phenomena coexist within a single mind, such that there is a "possessor" and that which is "possessed. Now, to sever this conceptualization, it is said that the mind alone is the possessor, and the three thousand realms of form and mind are what is possessed.

Just as with the eight phases of change, if objects were not divided into before and after, or if the characteristics existed prior to the object and the object existed prior to the characteristics, then the objects would not undergo transformation; it is only by discussing the transformation of the characteristics within the objects themselves that transformation occurs.
The phrase "merely shifting the characteristics to discuss phenomena" means that there is no before or after; thus it is said, "merely possessing [the nature].

This refers precisely to the passage on the inconceivable realm inherent in the mind within the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation). The *Zhiguan* states: "One thought-moment is the three thousand realms, and the three thousand realms are one thought-moment.
One thought-moment does not exist prior to the three thousand, and the three thousand do not exist subsequent to the one thought-moment. (Text: The Eight Aspects.)

There are four each of the "great" and "small" [characteristics], namely: birth (*jāti*), abiding (*sthiti*), change (*anyathātva*), and cessation (*anityatā*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains:

"The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the agents of transformation, while the phenomena (*dharma*) are the objects of transformation. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "This refers to 'birth-of-birth' (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth; they have efficacy with respect to eight and one respectively.

That is to say, the four primary characteristics and the four secondary characteristics are termed the "eight great characteristics," where the former are the primary and the latter are the secondary. This is because [the secondary characteristics] act upon them.
For eight reasons, all phenomena (dharmas) are established as having the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the statement "arising of arising" (*jāti-jāti*):

this refers to the "small arising" (*kṣudra-jāti*) which brings about the "great arising" (*mahā-jāti*) within the eight [conditioned characteristics]. Regarding "having capacity in one": this means that the small characteristic (*kṣudra-lakṣaṇa*) has the capacity to produce the great characteristic (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) within the one;

and the great characteristic has the capacity [to produce] within the eight. That is to say, when one great characteristic arises, it must necessarily arise together with three other great characteristics and four small characteristics.
Because the eight characteristics arise together with the fundamental dharma, it is said there are "eight characteristics"; the other three great characteristics are likewise so.
Thus, these eight characteristics, when compared to the fundamental dharma, are neither before nor after it; that the mind possesses the three thousand [realms] is likewise so.

The three thousand are like the eight characteristics, and the one mind is like the fundamental dharma (text). Furthermore, regarding the nature of the mind, it points back to the aforementioned "non-existence."
This non-mind nature—this three-thousandfold world of form and mind—is called "nature-virtue" (*prakṛti-guṇa*) because it cannot be altered whether in the causal state or the resultant state.
This first section concludes by establishing the general and the particular; regarding this principle, both the general and the particular take the phenomena of mindfulness as their generality.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the mind itself is called transformation," etc.: this refers to the aforementioned mind that possesses the three thousand [realms].

Following conditions—whether provisional or pure—it is unchanging yet undergoes transformation; it is not created, yet it creates. It is able to accomplish the phenomenal characteristics of the three thousand within the realm of cultivation.

Although this "transformation" also encompasses the distinct [teachings] and "creation" extends through all four [vehicles], here we specifically name the mind that possesses the three thousand as "transformation. If this "transformation" is termed "creation," then its nature belongs to the Perfect [Teaching].

These two phrases apply to all three teachings. Within the phenomenal realm (*dharma*), "totality" and "particularity" refer to the transformation and construction of the *three thousand* worlds as the particular, and the single moment of thought (*kṣaṇa-ekacitta*) as the total.
This is because the *three thousand* share a single nature; therefore, they all converge within a single moment of thought.

[Commentary] The explanation of "identifying the mind as transformation" and "naming the phenomena as totality and particularity": "Identifying the mind as transformation" reiterates the text; it refers to what follows above and below.

"Śì (釋)" means "to explain," which refers to the mind itself. This explains the passage from "the mind of a single moment endowed with all virtues" (*tathatā*) down to "transforming and creating" (*pariṇāma*).

It states that the nature of *tathatā* (Suchness), while remaining unchanging, is able to transform and create the phenomena of the ten realms according to the two conditions of defilement and purity.

Regarding "unchanging" (*abhinna*): because the entire nature transforms and creates, it is called "unchanging"; yet, although it does not undergo transformation, it nonetheless creates transformations. This explains the subsequent section.

The *Yìjīnbǐ* (Golden Scalpel of Meaning) explains "transformation" (*biàn*) as follows: Since there are only two meanings of "transformation," it is said to encompass both the particular (*bié*) and the universal (*tōng*).

While "construction" (*zào*) applies universally across the four collections (*sì zàng*), and although both "construction" and "transformation" apply universally, their specific meanings are restricted.

By taking the universal from the restricted, they are termed "transformation"; "transformation" is also termed "construction. Thus, all three meanings are complete. This [section] concludes the formation of the matter.
General and Particular.
[Commentary]: "To create" refers to essence and function; this points to the aforementioned transformation and creation, which is the totality of the essence giving rise to function.

Because the preceding mind already possesses both matter and mind, it transforms and creates matter and mind according to conditions during the stage of cultivation; thus, the three thousand [realms] within the nature serve as the essence of the matter and mind cultivated therein.

When cultivation brings forth the three thousand [realms] as function, the principle-body is fully manifested within phenomenal function; only then does this accord with the meaning of "following conditions" (suiyuan) in the Perfect Teaching.
Thus, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "The 'creation by mind' has two aspects: first, creation in terms of principle, which refers to 'endowment' (ju);

second, creation in terms of phenomena, which clarifies the transformations and creations of the three periods of time by ordinary beings and sages. It concludes by stating that all of these arise from principle.

"Is it appropriate for this text, which possesses the function of manifesting phenomena, to correspond back to that [principle]? [Explanation: "The term 'creation' (zào) refers to essence and function. The first phrase cites the text to point back to what precedes;
from 'up to the one who initiates function,' it provides a general heading. Therefore, the subsequent explanation is as follows:

'the mind previously possessed of matter and mind' points back to the principle-creation (li-zào); 'the matter and mind produced through conditions during cultivation' points back to the phenomenon-creation (shi-zào). Thus, by means of...

The latter two phrases explain the present essence and function; specifically, the latter two phrases clarify that the totality of the essence gives rise to function, which is precisely the meaning of "the unchanging following conditions" (*abhanga-anuvṛtti*) that constitutes the Perfect Teaching’s doctrine of "following conditions. Regarding the citations used as evidence for this identity:

first, in terms of principle (*li*), they are identical to the present mind’s manifestation as both matter and mind; second, in terms of phenomena (*shi*), they are identical to the present teaching that "mind itself is called transformation," and so forth.

All this arises because the principle is fully present, which then gives rise to phenomenal function; this is identical to what is called "creation" today. Thus, the two texts concerning essence and function are like two halves of a tally fitting together perfectly.
[Commentary] Question: The term "transformation" (bian) originally derives from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, where it says: "inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation."

The term "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) originally derives from the *Avataṃsaka*, where it says, "creating various kinds of the five aggregates. Thus, in the *Avataṃsaka*, there are only two doctrines, whereas in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, all four doctrines are combined. Why, then, does the *Jinbi* (Golden Needle) state that the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is limited to two [doctrines], while "creation" applies to all four? Answer: Although the number of doctrines contained within each section is indeed as stated, here we are considering the difference between the universal and the restricted scope of their literal meanings. Why? 1. Regarding "transformation," the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of "transforming the six sense objects into the three vehicles," which refers to the transformation of the external world. The *Laṅkāvatāra* speaks of "the transformation of consciousness," which refers to the transformation of the internal mind. Since these two refer to different things, they are not combined into one. 2. Regarding "creation," although the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of "creating various kinds of the five aggregates," this refers to the creation of the five aggregates by sentient beings themselves. The *Laṅkāvatāra* speaks of "the Tathāgata’s creation of the five aggregates," which refers to the Buddha’s creation of the five aggregates for the sake of sentient beings. Since these two refer to different agents, they are not combined into one. 3. Regarding "nature-arising" (*xingqi*), the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of "the nature-arising of the five aggregates," which refers to the arising of the five aggregates from the nature of reality. The *Laṅkāvatāra* speaks of "the nature-arising of the eight consciousnesses," which refers to the arising of the eight consciousnesses from the nature of reality. Since these two refer to different phenomena, they are not combined into one. 4. Regarding "true thusness" (*tathatā*), the *Avataṃsaka* speaks of "true thusness creating the five aggregates," which refers to true thusness creating the five aggregates for sentient beings. The *Laṅkāvatāra* speaks of "true thusness transforming the eight consciousnesses," which refers to true thusness transforming the eight consciousnesses for sentient beings. Since these two refer to different functions, they are not combined into one. Therefore, although the number of doctrines in each section is as stated, the distinction here is based on the difference between the universal and restricted scope of their literal meanings. Why? Because the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Laṅkāvatāra* do not mutually include one another’s specific terminology. For example, the *Avataṃsaka* mentions "transformation" but not "creation"; the *Laṅkāvatāra* mentions "creation" but not "transformation. Generally speaking, "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is mostly named according to the shifting and turning of the entity itself; thus, the term "transformation" is restrictive.

However, when discussing "creation" (*nirmāṇa*), there is both creation as transformation and creation as accumulation. Therefore, the term "creation" is comprehensive, encompassing both the Shared and Distinct teachings, as they all possess the nature of the central reality (*madhyama-tattva*).
Thus, the two teachings (Shared and Distinct) point to transformation as creation. The Tripitaka and Shared teachings [likewise] do so.
Since there is no substantial essence within, it merely clarifies that karma and delusion construct all phenomena; it does not speak of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).

In the Mahayana, it is "mind-only," while in the Hinayana, because [phenomena] arise from the mind, it speaks of "transformation. Thus, "only two" refers to transformation, while "constructing all" applies to all four [schools]. [Commentary]:

This distinguishes between "transformation" and "construction" regarding the function produced and that which produces it. It refers to the two sūtras; as for the function produced, it is like the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel), which primarily addresses the specific schools.

The *Zhong* (the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*) details the extent of the teachings to challenge the principle that the inconceivable permeation is inherently complete; as it says, "True Suchness internally permeates.

The *Fuxing* (the *Fuxing zhuan*) states, "True Suchness constantly permeates, and [the nature] is internally complete. It is also said that "inconceivable transformation through old permeation" refers to the creation of phenomena (*shizao*).

Because the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* belongs to the Vaipulya (Equivalence) category, it contains all four teachings. The *Jinbi* (The Golden Needle) states that the meaning of "transformation" consists of only two types.
Regarding the phrase "now, 'etcetera'" and so forth, this refers to the response concerning the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).

It means that one does not discuss it based on the quantity of teachings contained within a specific section, but rather explains it by way of the general or specific scope of the literal meaning of the characters. First, the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) is explained: "transformation" means a shifting transformation;
because the true nature of the Middle Way is wondrously indeterminate, it undergoes perfuming and transformation, which signifies the sense of its own essence being altered and turned. This...

Since even the Buddhas of others' past and future lives are identical with the mind, how much more so the Buddhas of one's own past and future lives—how could they ever deviate from a single thought-moment? [Commentary]: The three thousand realms of principle and phenomena are fully present within the mind; they are inherently possessed.

Because it transforms the function of the entire substance, one should know that simply realizing the present moment as the general principle of all phenomena allows for the universal vision of the three thousand realms of principle and fact, of self and others, and of sentient beings and Buddhas.
The nine realms constitute "sentient beings" and the ultimate fruit constitutes "Buddha. That the mind possesses the ten realms is called "one's own sentient beings and Buddha";
that each of these sentient beings and Buddhas individually possesses the ten realms is called "the sentient beings and Buddhas of others."
Using others to illustrate oneself, it is said that even the three thousandfold world of the Buddhas and sentient beings—so vast and lofty—is identical to the mind;
how much more so for that which is inherently possessed within one's own mind, which could not possibly deviate from a single thought-moment.

[Commentary] "One's own Buddhas and sentient beings" refers to the three thousandfold world of the mind-dharma; "the Buddhas and sentient beings of others" refers to the Buddha-dharma and the sentient-being dharma. Both are...

This is called "each possessing three thousand [realms] within themselves. These three thousand do not arise apart from the Buddha, for by principle they encompass phenomena, tending toward the same destination as my own mind;
this is because they are the equipment of the mind, because they are transformations of the mind, and because they are the total embodiment of its function.

Therefore, in a single thought-moment of consciousness, one is able to see them all-pervasively. [Commentary]: The explanation states that "by principle they encompass phenomena" means that the inherent principle encompasses and attains the phenomena.
Since the principle is fully realized, the phenomena are encompassed by the raising of a single instance; thus, within the realm of phenomena, all things converge in a single moment of thought.
This interpretation holds that by knowing a single moment of thought, one universally perceives the Buddhas and sentient beings of both oneself and others.
△ Third, "Therefore, those [below]" concludes the non-duality.
Thus, although the various phenomena of each respective object differ, they do not differ. [Commentary: This concludes the aforementioned non-duality.

Regarding the phrase "those respective [objects]," since the distinctions between self and other, birth and Buddhahood, delusion and awakening, and high and low, within the realms of objects, are all one and the same mind, it is said that they "differ" yet... [do not differ].
"It is not erroneous.
[Commentary] It can be seen that he says this original text contains one extra character "chā" (差); whether it is retained or omitted makes no difference, so there is no need for strenuous dispute.

Furthermore, the Master of Wuming (Wen) held that there is no fixed standard for what to retain or omit.
