The names "Three Nirvāṇas" and "Three Dharmas" explain below that cause and effect are not distinct; the cause is named the Three Tracks (trivartman), and the fruit is named the Three Dharmas of Nirvāṇa.
The essence of these Three Dharmas is eternally unchanging.
△ Second, "If this were so," and below, [discusses] the difference between the phenomena of delusion and awakening. Part one: the intent of the question.

If this is so, and the causes and virtues are already complete, why does one not abide in the cause? [Commentary: The section on "the difference between the phenomena of delusion and awakening" intends to manifest that cause and effect are non-dual;
first, it distinguishes the particularity of the phenomena of delusion and awakening. Only when these phenomena are distinguished can the principle that they are non-dual yet dual be revealed.
Because "two yet not two," cause and effect are provisionally distinguished based on delusion and enlightenment.

If this is so, the intent of the question—arising from the realization that the causal mind is inherently endowed with [the three tracks]—is as follows: since the causal mind already possesses the three tracks, it is the very nature of the person who attains the fruit;
why then should one abide only in the cause and seek the fruit?
[Commentary]: Seeking to realize the stage of fruition is for the sake of accomplishing the causes and virtues; once these virtues are complete, why seek the fruition?
△ Second, "But by... and so forth, answers the underlying intent:

It is merely because of delusion regarding the cause that each person claims it to be real. If one understands the nature of delusion, one truly abides only in the cause; therefore, one has long investigated this.

"Because causes manifest through causes, they are called fruits. [Commentary] In the response, one should first state: "If one were to realize that the nature of delusion is truly nothing but abiding in the cause," yet for now, the faults of that which is deluded are first shown;
thus it says, "It is solely due to delusion regarding the cause that each person claims it to be real.

To say "it is real" means that dharmas are fundamentally empty and harmonious, yet sentient beings, in their subjective sentiments, grasp them as real. One wishes to depart from this sentiment of taking things to be real.
Because one practices without ceasing, it is said that through long-term study this cause is realized; when emotional attachments vanish and virtue manifests, the name of the fruit is established.
Thus it is said: "The cause being manifest, the fruit is named.
[Commentary] Although the virtues of the cause are complete, while still in a state of delusion, one grasps at the fundamental fusion of all phenomena as being real; starting from this point...
From the Avīci Hell up to the Vajra-peak, all possess this thought; yet if one does not consider it real, the iron bed is not suffering, and there is no transformation or transition.
When this thought is exhausted, it is called "Wondrous Enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that each considers their own [state] to be real.
If one realizes the nature of what was deluded, what separate Buddha-fruit could there be? One merely returns to realize the virtue of the cause; hence it is said, "abiding in the cause."
Because the names of the fruits are received according to the locus where virtues are manifested, the phenomena are distinguished as distinct based on delusion and enlightenment. [Commentary:

Regarding the initial explanation that "it is simply due to delusion regarding the cause that each person individually claims it to be real, while all dharmas are fundamentally fused," this means that the three thousand dharmas are fundamentally all empty and fused;
the mind of ignorance grasps them as being real, as it is said: "A single form, a single fragrance—none are not [thus]."
For sentient beings of the middle way, their sentiments are obstructed from the Subtle [Ear]; this is what is meant by "the true mind.
Beginning from the Avīci hell and ending with the final moment of mind at the Vajra stage, although delusions may vary in thickness, all possess this thought.

If one does not regard it as real and so forth, it is because the absence makes the presence manifest—just as the iron bed is contrasted with the preceding Avīci, and the transformation-death (pariṇāma-maraṇa) is contrasted with the preceding Vajra stage; if this were not present...

The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are *anabhini* (non-arising), yet they are not causes of suffering; they shift and transform, yet they do not transmigrate. There is nothing that is not thoroughly exhausted;
only when one is free from conceptualization regarding the "real mind" is it called wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). If one understands this, it explains the following:

if one understands the nature of delusion, etc., then once the nature of the three tracks (*trivartman*) which are the objects of delusion is understood, there is no separate Buddha-fruit produced from elsewhere. As the ancient masters said: "It is simply returning to the original source."
At that time, in terms of nature (*dharmatā*), not a single dharma is newly produced.
△ Third, "merely by conditions" (*pratyaya*) clarifies that phenomena reach their limit and principle vanishes.
Merely by conditions, cause and principle are one; using this single principle as the cause, the principle is manifested and the name of "fruit" no longer exists—how could it be otherwise?
If the cause still persists, then the name remains; once cause and effect have vanished, the principle of nature naturally perishes. [Commentary:

This is because the preceding and subsequent causes and effects are no different, and the principle from beginning to end is one. Since the single principle is taken as the cause, it is also taken as the fruit;

this is because the cause and effect of the Mahāyāna are both the true mark (*dharmatā*). When the principle is manifested, both cause and effect vanish together, for the principle itself also dissolves.

Knowing cause and effect is the activity of grasping at phenomena (*dharma*). Once the principle (*li*) is attained, phenomena vanish; since the nature (*xing*) is that which can integrate the single principle, it too vanishes of its own accord.

[Commentary] Regarding "the principle manifests," etc.: in contrast to what is hidden, it is called the "cause," and what is manifest is called the "effect. Once manifested, there is no longer a name for the effect in contrast to it.
How could the capacity for the fruit exist when even the name "real" no longer exists? Since the cause already belongs to the provisional, both should be abandoned.
Furthermore, since the phenomena of cause and fruit are established in opposition to one another, once that which is opposed has vanished, that which opposes it naturally perishes.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "opposing the hidden," this explains that when the principle is revealed, the name "fruit" no longer exists. Because the name is hidden, it is called "cause"; because the name is revealed, it is called "fruit. This is as explained previously.

When the thousand true marks (*sahasra-lakṣaṇa*) have not yet manifested, they are called the cause; once manifested, they are called the fruit. This is a discussion of cause and fruit based on the relative opposition of concealment and manifestation.

If the rational nature (*li-xing*) were manifested, there would be no concealment left to oppose it; thus, the name "fruit" would cease to exist. Since the fruit cannot exist [in that state], how could the designation of "cause" remain?

Furthermore, since the reality of the fruit does not exist, the provisional means of the cause are likewise abolished. Moreover, regarding the subsequent two lines of the commentary below, the cause is discussed in contrast to the fruit.
The fruit is the phenomenon and its single nature is the principle; by using the principle to harmonize the phenomenon, both cause and effect vanish.
Since that which is countered has vanished, that which harmonizes also dissolves.
△ Second, "Precisely because of" and below, clarifying that there is no attainment in cultivation and realization based on perfect understanding. Part one: Clarifying delusion by means of the Dharma.
The essence of wisdom is fundamentally empty;

it is only because one loses track of wisdom’s intimacy or distance that delusion becomes thick or thin. Because delusion is thick or thin, one forcibly distinguishes the three afflictions, establishes the meaning of the six stages of realization, and designates the varying depths of wisdom.

[Commentary] It is said that the "wisdom that transcends words" is precisely the wisdom in which both phenomena and principle are suddenly extinguished; because it is able to effect a perfect severance, it is said:

"It is solely by virtue of the Perfect Person’s use of non-referential wisdom from beginning to end that all dharmas are suddenly extinguished. Since even the principle and its fruit are extinguished, how could there be successive delusions?
It is solely due to the subtle or manifest power of this wisdom that there arise distinctions of remoteness and intimacy; and because of these distinctions of remoteness and intimacy..."
The delusions that fall away before or after [realization] are termed "thick" or "thin"; wisdom is distant when delusion is thick, and wisdom is intimate when delusion is thin.

These distinctions are clarified through successive transmission; this is how delusions are categorized according to wisdom. Since there is the principle of thickness and thinness, the three delusions are forcibly divided. Furthermore, based on this meaning, they are opened up into six stages of identity (*liu-ji*).

If one speaks of the extinction of wisdom, it refers to the realization of the principle of identity (*ji-li*); however, if one discusses the shallowness or depth of wisdom, it refers to the extinction of ignorance.

There is not a single virtue to be cultivated, nor a single delusion to be destroyed; yet we forcibly name them "thick or thin," "shallow or deep. [Commentary] The substance of both delusion and wisdom is fundamentally empty.
Although wisdom has degrees of intimacy and distance, when delusion becomes thick or thin, one realizes that its substance is identical to principle and fundamentally empty—this is "fusion" (*rong*).
In the first section of the *Chao*, the two types of perfect severance (*yuan-duan*) are indicated; from "merely by" (*zhiyou xia*) onwards, they are distinguished according to wisdom.

Regarding the third delusion: if one discusses the subsequent conclusion that returns to the perfect severance of delusions, this refers to the wisdom in which the aforementioned phenomena and principle are suddenly extinguished.
"Phenomena" being extinguished refers to the fact that cause and effect have already vanished; "principle" being naturally extinguished refers to the fact that the nature of reality itself vanishes.

For a practitioner of the Perfect Sudden Teaching, they establish contemplation based upon the objective realm such that subject and object are both extinguished; beginning from the stage of "name and word" and continuing through to the stage of Equal Enlightenment, it is thus at every level.
Therefore, it is said that from beginning to end, absolute wisdom is employed; not only are cause and effect extinguished, but even the pure principle of nature (li-xing) vanishes.
Thus it is said that all dharmas are suddenly obliterated. If even the principle of the fruit is obliterated, this is spoken of in terms of its preeminence, setting aside the discussion of the cause.
As for the "principle of the fruit," since this is the actual substance realized, it itself vanishes; how much more so the afflictive obstructions, which are merely that which is to be destroyed?

How could deluded sentiments possibly maintain a sequence? If that is so, why is it that the afflictions of view-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), thought-delusion (*bhāvanā-heya*), dust-and-sand-like delusions, and ignorance (*avidyā*) possess degrees of coarseness and subtlety, thickness and thinness?
It is said: "It is solely because of this [equality]. Because the power of the wisdom that suddenly causes these phenomena and principles to vanish is slight, it is called "distant";

because they are manifest, they are called "intimate. The *Chao* (Commentary) explains the meaning of "intimate" and "distant" through "slight" and "manifest": since the wisdom is distant, [the afflictions are intimate].
Because the wisdom that eliminates the heavy delusions of the prior stage is proximate, the light delusions fall away later; this is clarified through successive transmission.

This is because, from the stage of "Similarity" (samyaktva-niyāma-avakrānti) onwards, the power of the contemplation is subtle as it relates to the distant [delusions]. Thus, among the three types of delusion within a single essence, those that are coarse fall away first; they receive the names "view-delusions" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and "affliction-delusions" (*kleśa-kleśa*) according to their strength.

From the stage of "Partial Truth" (*bhūta-tattva*) upwards, because the power of the contemplation is proximate and manifest, the subtle aspects of the three types of delusion within a single essence [are eliminated].

Now, while severing [delusion], one may provisionally apply the designation "ignorance" (avidyā) to that which is predominant; yet, once the true nature is realized, one may further discuss the relative intimacy and distance, as well as the degree of thickness and thinness, across the successive stages.
Because delusion has degrees of thickness, the three afflictions are forcibly distinguished; thus, they are distinguished where there was no distinction.
Because wisdom has degrees of depth, the doctrine opens into the six levels of realization; thus, distinctions are made where there should have been none. There is no error here.

This discusses the relative depth within the context of both the shallow and the deep. If one understands through the perfect, interfused, and non-referential wondrous contemplation (*prajñā*) that afflictions and wisdom are fundamentally empty—since wisdom is identical to principle (*tattva*), there is no virtue to be cultivated;

since afflictions are identical to principle, there is no affliction to be destroyed—then this cultivation of virtue without effort is the practice of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*), which alone is called "perfect severance. The meaning of perfect severance is as explained in the fourth chapter of the *Yichuanyiji*.
Furthermore, the *Jingjue Lengyan* (Pure Enlightenment Śūraṅgama) states in its title:

"It is solely because the power of contemplation differs in being weak or profound that those who are coarse fall first, while those who are subtle break through later; this is not due to deliberate effort, but occurs spontaneously. Zhuan’an’s Supplementary Notes state:

"This refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which first severs the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and subsequently severs ignorance (*avidyā*); this is explained in terms of the power of contemplation."
It is traditionally said that a predecessor once asked: "If the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is slight, all [afflictions] are slight; if it is prominent, all are prominent.
Why then do the delusions to be destroyed not simultaneously and proportionally break apart according to the power of the three contemplations? This questioner truly has insight.
Now it is said that for a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), everything is perfectly interfused; the delusions to be destroyed are merely biased attachments (*pian-qing*). Bias...

Because the emotions (afflictions) are coarse or subtle, there is a sequence of priority; traditionally, scholars have held that while the Dharma is difficult to fathom and perfectly explicates all phenomena as entirely interfused, it is only due to biased emotions that one forcibly distinguishes them into the three delusions.

△ Second, as explained below through analogies, it is clarified that the merit of cultivation and realization is not established as two. First, it clarifies that the merit of cultivation and realization is non-existent.

Thus, as in a dream, diligent effort in the empty name [of phenomena] severs delusion; once the illusory cause is fulfilled, the mirror-image fruit is perfected. [Commentary: This is intended to clarify...

Because the merit of cultivation and realization has vanished, the four metaphors of dreams, emptiness, illusions, and images are employed to illustrate that both the cause and fruit of wisdom and abandonment are accomplished through non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
The diligent cultivation of the virtue of wisdom accords with the nature of reality; thus, like events in a dream, they are ultimately unattainable.
Delusive afflictions are fundamentally non-existent and merely nominal, lacking substantiality, just as empty space exists only as a name. Like an illusion, it penetrates all things.

This is used as an analogy for the function of superior wisdom and abandonment; thus, it is restated that "once the mirror is full, images appear within it," which serves as a metaphor for the perfection of the fruits and virtues.

[The Sub-commentary] states: Others say that dreams, emptiness, illusions, and images—these four are all metaphors used to explain the meaning by correlating them with wisdom, abandonment, cause, and effect.

Although this does not explicitly clarify the *Abhidharma*, it somewhat corresponds to it; furthermore, it is said that below the section on "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), one must apply this name, as its meaning is very convenient.
This is because it states that the essence of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is like empty space, existing only as a name. Thus, the fourth of the Ten Similes of the Mahāyāna says:
"As for empty space, emptiness exists only as a name and lacks any reality," and so forth. This is the intended meaning of the character *míng* (name).
Although my explanations are numerous, I fear they have not yet reached the essence; now I merely intend to clarify the principles—how could I dare to show partiality toward my own sentiments?
As for my own view: if any character in the old texts possesses even a slight degree of reason, I shall follow it accordingly.

Should the holy eyes of the sages clearly perceive my heart, yet if my wisdom is deficient and my words too sparse to fully accord with the truth, I beg the great masters to provide me with correction and rebuke.

Now, the reason these four metaphors are cited is to reveal that for the person of perfect realization (*paripūrṇa-pudgala*), wondrous understanding is fundamentally endowed with all virtues and myriad delusions are inherently empty;

thus, although the stages of realization and cultivation are established, each is without effortful action (*anābhoga*). Therefore, one diligently cultivates the practice of wisdom as if performing actions in a dream, wherein nothing at all is discerned.
Delusions are merely names, like space, lacking any reality; knowing them to be thus, they are immediately severed. This is further explained in terms of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
From beginning to end, because the cause lacks the power to induce [an effect], it is like an illusion; because the effect is not something that can be produced, it is like a reflection.
Since the understanding is already in accord with reality, all four are without action. If this is so for both cause and effect, how could there be duality?

[Commentary] The first part narrates the views of others; the second, "Now," introduces the present explanation. The first of these [the narration of others' views] is further divided into two parts. First, he presents their response; the text has been revised here.

Regarding these two characters, they are now merely presented below to indicate that one should now act so as to eliminate the mind of emotional attachment. As for the phrase "and so forth" (*tad-ādi*), the *Zhuǐ* (Pointing Out) states:

"The four metaphors herein are as follows: the dream metaphor represents wisdom (*jñāna*), the emptiness metaphor represents abandonment (*prahāṇa*), the illusion metaphor represents the cause (*hetu*), and the image metaphor represents the fruit (*phala*').
To speak of 'exerting oneself as in a dream' is precisely a metaphor for the wisdom capable of eliminating [attachment]. It is like a dream which is fundamentally non-existent due to sleep."

Because of the mind, there is perception; yet once one seeks it within a dream, it is unobtainable, while the events of the dream remain vividly present. All phenomena are fundamentally empty, yet they exist due to ignorance (*avidyā*).

If wisdom (*jñāna*) is developed, the nature [of things] is seen to be originally non-existent. Because one contemplates only this absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is said that through diligent application, the name "emptiness" itself ceases to delude;
this is a metaphor for the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Ignorance has no substantial reality from the beginning, existing only as a phantom.

The term "cause of illusion" (māyā-hetu) serves as a general metaphor for the causes of both wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). As for the "mirror-image," it refers to an image within a mirror;

by not taking the mirror itself but taking only the image, it is meant to illustrate that the fruit (*phala*) is unobtainable. (Text) Regarding the necessity of applying this name [“darkness”] below the section on emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

the claim that there is another version of the text where this reads “darkness” (*ming*) is a mistaken emendation made by later generations. The intended meaning is that it signifies "dark resonance" (*mingqi*), referring to a profound accord with reality.

Because it is the principle of true emptiness, it is said that delusions are severed. Now, I say this is not so; for it is not only that the dharma and the metaphor are not distinguished, but one is also ignorant of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
(Text) In the "Ten Similes" of the Mahāyāna, the general preface to the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* praises the merits of the bodhisattvas, saying:
"They understand all dharmas to be like an illusion, like a mirage, like the moon in water, like space, and like an echo."
It is like a city of the gandharvas, like a dream, like a shadow, like an image in a mirror, and like a transformation.

The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Space has only a name but lacks reality" (text). Second, the explanation of the present [topic] has three parts: first, a general indication of the four meanings; second, from "therefore, with diligence...
onwards, a detailed explanation of the four metaphors; third, from "once understood... onwards, a conclusion that returns to non-duality. First sentence.

The general summary of all virtues fundamentally reveals the intent of diligent application as being like a dream; it shows that the myriad delusions are originally empty, and thus the name "delusion" ceases.
Regarding the myriad delusions, the layers of ignorance (*avidyā*) are exceedingly numerous, as explained in various places regarding the "Samādhi of Breaking Ignorance.

Furthermore, it is said that the sands of the Ganges' afflictions are realized through the cultivation of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), which indicates the illusory cause as being like a mirror-image. This is followed by the specific distinctions.
In the commentary, the lower three phrases explain the practice of wisdom through the metaphor of a dream; this refers to the virtue of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇa*). The phrase "afflictions are merely...
and the following three phrases explain the metaphor of emptiness; this refers to the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

"Knowing they are non-existent is to sever them" means that one understands afflictions have only names and lack reality; thus, they are termed "severed. Furthermore, the lower four phrases explain the metaphor of illusory images.
The beginning of wisdom and severance is the cause; the end of wisdom and severance is the fruit. That which can accomplish is the cause, and that which is achieved is the fruit.

All are explained by combining the Dharma with metaphors. Since the perfect understanding within the section on the Severing of Bonds accords with the true principle, it causes the wondrous practice of realization and cultivation to manifest non-action, revealing that cause and fruit are non-dual.
△ Second, the two types of empty images clarify that the substance of the obstacles differs.

Although the "empty image" and the "identical meaning" are the same in name, they differ in substance: the empty image is void, whereas the identical image is real. Thus, it is said that the principle fundamentally possesses emptiness;

because it is void, delusion evolves into the nature [of the obstacle]. [Commentary]: The first phrase cites and indicates that while the meanings of "empty" and "identical" are the same, there is only a name; the mirror-image lacks inherent nature.

Therefore, while the meaning of "unreal" is the same as in the preceding phrase, this sentence briefly indicates a difference in essence. For the Perfect Person (*yuanren*), the obstacles themselves are virtues;

why then speak of a difference in essence? What is meant here by "difference" is the essence of their fundamental substance (*zhiti*). It is spoken of as "different" from a general perspective based on the distinction between delusion and enlightenment.

[Commentary]: Although the meaning of emptiness regarding delusions, images, and fruits—as being unreal—is the same, "emptiness" refers merely to names, for while knowledge of non-existence is eternally severed, images, though lacking intrinsic nature, possess distinct color-forms;
thus it is said that "emptiness is void while images are real. Regarding the phrase "images are real," etc., this explains that the substance is different:
the three thousand virtues of the fruit are not something newly attained at this time, and therefore the treatise does not claim they are unreal. This is called the "reality of images."

Because the fundamental source is realized as being incapable of extinction, it is said that "in accordance with principle, it is inherently existent. When there is delusion, it is precisely ignorance;

because ignorance is transformed, it immediately changes into clarity. Since the name "delusion" is forever lost and it becomes the intrinsic clarity of nature, it is said that "delusion is transformed into nature.
Others say that one must speak of "nature becoming [clarity]. If one says "becoming nature," it would cause the fruit to become the cause. If that were so...

The subsequent text states: "If one realizes that present ignorance is the *dharmatā*, does this not mean that the effect also becomes the cause? [Commentary] The first part provides the correct explanation;
the second cites the views of former masters to refute them. Regarding the initial point: "emptiness" is the metaphor for delusion (*moha*), while "images" are the metaphor for the fruit.
Delusion is the obstacle to be eliminated; the fruit is the virtue to be manifested. As for "unreal," it refers to what was stated above: delusion is merely...
Names are like space, lacking substantial fruit because they cannot be realized; they are like reflections. The following section from "Emptiness" explains the second phrase:
"The empty void and the reflection are real"—this briefly indicates the difference in their essential natures. To know that there is no [substantial] existence is to eternally sever [delusion];

that is, once one knows that names have no substance, they naturally and eternally cease, and there is nothing further to exist. Although the reflection has no inherent nature, the reflection appearing within a mirror is not... [the text ends here].

Arising from the departure of both self and other, although devoid of intrinsic nature, the characteristics of form are manifestly present. Regarding the fruit of virtue, the third phrase is explained below:
it explains that the fruit of virtue, which is manifested as the perfected reality, is the primordial nature that has always been present;

its cultivation through practice is not something newly acquired now, for cultivation is subsumed by nature. Thus, the treatise states that the fruit is not as previously [described], for the fruit is not something to be newly achieved. Fruit.
Since virtue accords with the nature (*dharmatā*) and the realization of that nature is called "unchanging," how could it ever be extinguished?
To explain the fourth phrase, "delusion" refers to when one takes the *dharmatā* to be ignorance; "awakening" refers to when one transforms ignorance into the luminosity of the nature.

This is called a transformation of the name, not a transformation of the substance. When delusion is said to be "permanently lost," it is as previously understood: the absence of [delusion] is eternally severed.
Regarding the phrase "He says, etc.," the *Zhuzhi* states: "There is a version that reads 'perfected nature' (*chengxing*), which is an error.

If it were so, it would conversely cause the fruit to become the cause; it would not be the case that the causal nature produces the fruit of wisdom. (Text) One can see that this refutes [the error] by citing the subsequent passage.
△ Third, this section below explains, in terms of the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-sheng), that the beginning and the end are non-dual. Part One: Reversing and responding to clarify that the essence is one.

Thus, although it is non-dual, it is dual in establishing the distinction between cause and effect; yet although it is dual, it is non-dual in that the essence of the beginning and the end is one. If one were to say...

The cause is distinct from the effect, yet the cause is not [itself] the cause; one must understand that the effect arises from the cause, and only through the cause does the effect finally achieve its realization. [Commentary:

The phrase "this is then" follows the meaning of the preceding text. Since the substance of virtue and obstruction is distinct—like the void and empty images versus the real—then the cause and effect are established as separate.
Now, clarifying that cause and effect are non-dual, one should further understand that while they are two, they are non-dual, being identical in essence from beginning to end.

First, if one says that the subsequent [passage] is a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) clarifying non-duality, then [the statement] "understanding that the fruit arises from the cause" and so forth is indeed concordant (*anuloma*).
[The *Commentary*] is easily understood.
△ Second, the passage beginning with "Because... clarifies non-duality by showing that there is no decrease despite being high and vast.

Therefore, when the three thousand realms abide in principle, they are all equally termed ignorance; when the three thousand realms are realized as the fruit, they are all called eternal and blissful.
Since the three thousand realms undergo no change, ignorance is itself enlightenment; the three thousand realms are all eternally so, sharing both the same substance and the same function.

[Commentary]: The cause and effect of the Mahāyāna are both the true aspect (*dharmatā*). All three thousand realms are the true aspect; the characteristics of the true aspect are manifest and complete.

When the true aspect exists as a principle, it acts as the cause for defilement; even if one possesses the Buddha-dharmas, because they have not yet been manifested, they are collectively termed ignorance (*avidyā*).

When the three thousand realms are free from hindrances and the eight inversions do not arise, every single dharma-gate accomplishes the four virtues; therefore, all are eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

The three thousand real aspects are all of an unchanging nature; the principles of delusion and awakening are identical, just as when Yajñadatta lost his head and found it again, the head was never different [from before].
Therefore, it is said that ignorance is itself enlightenment. Each and every thing within the three thousand worlds is eternally abiding;

the inherent possession of the three thousand is collectively termed "substance" (*tǐ*), while the transformative manifestation of the three thousand is collectively termed "function" (*yòng*). Thus it is said:
Regarding these four propositions concerning both essence and function: the first two clarify that cause and effect each possess the three thousand;
the third clarifies that the three thousand of cause and effect are in fact one single three thousand, because there is no alteration;

and the fourth clarifies that the essence of the three thousand of cause and effect is equally capable of giving rise to function—such that the three thousand within the causal state give rise to defiled functions, while the three thousand at the stage of fruition give rise to [pure functions].
Regarding the "Pure Function. [Commentary: The section explaining that the three thousand realms abide within principle as being high and vast without decrease means:

"high" refers to the fruit of the Buddha-realm, and "vast" refers to the cause of sentient beings. Although high and vast differ, their essence neither increases nor decreases; therefore, cause and effect are non-dual.
Having first provided a general explanation of the four propositions, this sutra now briefly elucidates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. As it says:
Since these characteristics are themselves the three thousand [realms], the three thousand are now explained here in terms of the true aspect (*dharmatā*) of cause and effect.
That both cause and effect are the true aspect is stated in the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*: "The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true aspect of all phenomena.

The Patriarch added the term "Mahāyāna" for the sake of the meaning: "The fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true aspect. Thus, all three thousand are the true aspect, and their characteristics remain perfectly distinct.
This means that the ten realms are inherently complete and are all true dharmas; because they never lose their own essence, it is said that "the true aspect is clearly present.

The following explains the first phrase: the three thousand realms exist within delusion regarding the principle, and because they can follow defiled conditions to produce the dharmas of the nine realms, it is said that "they act as causes for defilement.
Within these three thousand realms, it is not that the Buddha-realm is absent, yet it has not been fully realized.
Because they are [yet to be] manifest, they are both termed "ignorance" (avidyā). Conventionally, it is said that the first phrase pertains to principle; however, here we rely on the cause.

From the stage of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the true reality remains unmanifest, and thus it is termed the "causal" [ignorance]. This collectively encompasses the five preceding stages, as even at Equal Enlightenment, ignorance has not been exhausted and the three thousand realms have not been fully realized;
because they are yet to be manifest, they are both termed "ignorance. The following section on the "three thousand" explains the next point.

Regarding the eight inversions of the phrases: the external heterodox views take false permanence and so forth as their realm; the four inversions of the Two Vehicles take impermanence as their realm;
and the four inversions of the ultimate fruit consist of the fact that every single dharma-gate realized therein is characterized by the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

However, by citing only "permanence" and "bliss," the presence of "self" and "purity" is understood by implication. [This concludes] the third section of the three thousand [lines], as explained below.
The three phrases explain the three thousand realms through their unchanging nature: delusion is precisely the cause and awakening is precisely the fruit.

Although delusion and awakening differ, the principle from beginning to end is one. Because the substance of delusion—namely ignorance—and the substance of awakening—namely inherent clarity—are non-dual, they are said to be "precisely" (ji) each other;
thus, ignorance is precisely clarity, and the principle of delusion and awakening is one. Losing one's head is a metaphor for delusion; regaining one's head is a metaphor for awakening.

The Fourth Section of the Awakening of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: Consider the case of Yajñadatta, who one morning looked into a mirror and, seeing the eyes, brows, and features of his head reflected therein, became enraged that his own head could not see its own face.
Thinking it to be a malevolent spirit (*chi-mei*), he ran about wildly in a state of madness.
Suddenly his madness subsided; yet his head was never obtained from without, so even if his madness had not ceased, what would he have lost? (Text: Yajñadatta)
[The section] "Reversing the Altar" explains the third [thousand worlds]; the section "The World Below" explains the fourth phrase.

First, it explains that the three thousand worlds are all eternally present, which corresponds to the "eternal nature of the world's characteristics" in the current sutra. Next, under the heading "Principle-Endowment," it explains that both essence and function are present. Question:

Now you say that the three thousand worlds as principle-endowed constitute the essence (*tǐ*), while the three thousand worlds as transformed creation constitute the function (*yòng*). Is this not because their principles are identical? Thus, it corresponds to the two [aspects].
Question: "What are the three thousand? Answer: It is precisely when one clarifies the total function of the Perfect Teaching (*en-ga*) that it is called "non-duality.

Regarding these four [categories] below, they collectively judge the four phrases; the first two clarify that cause and effect each possess the three thousand, thereby showing that the first phrase includes the previous five [categories] within the three thousand of the causal stage.

[Commentary] This fourth phrase clarifies that the Perfect [Teaching] is most manifest. Why is this? For the names "essence" (tǐ) and "function" (yòng) are fundamentally based on the principle of mutual identity.

Therefore, when it is said that all phenomena are identical with the Principle, it is only when function is entirely identical with essence that one can speak of "identity. As the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:
"Regarding 'identity' (jí), the *Guangya* says it means 'union. If one relies on this interpretation, it still seems as though two distinct things are being joined together."
This principle is still somewhat remote; now, seeking it through its meaning, because the essence is non-dual, it is called "immediate" (*ji*). (The above is explanatory prose.

Now, I maintain that only when the function of the entire essence manifests can it be called non-dual. In other schools, it is explained that the single principle follows conditions to produce differentiated phenomena, and these differentiations are the marks of ignorance (*avidyā*).
That which is pure and unitary is the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*). When following conditions...

Thus, there is differentiation when following conditions, but no differentiation when not following conditions; therefore, we know that it is only when the single nature combines with ignorance that differentiation arises.
This is precisely the meaning of "combination," rather than the two being non-dual in essence, because when ignorance is removed, there is no differentiation.
Our school clarifies that while the essence of the three thousand dharmas follows conditions to give rise to the function of the three thousand, it does not itself follow conditions.
At that time, the three thousandfold world-system is as it is; thus, the differentiated phenomena and their essence are non-dual.
Because the existence of differentiation is removed through the elimination of ignorance, the proof of the other school’s principle—that manifestation is itself the essence—is not established.

This is because that Buddha-fruit is solely True Suchness (tathatā), which must break through the differentiation of the nine realms to return to the single nature of the Buddha-realm. [Commentary] Explanation of the first part of the fourth phrase.

By clarifying the principle of "identity" (*ji*) through the non-duality of essence and function, it is stated that both are essence and both are function; this precisely reveals the non-duality of essence and function.

Since it simultaneously clarifies both transformation and manifestation, it fully elucidates the intent of mutual identity. Therefore, it is said to be "most manifest. (The *Fuxingwen* [Commentary on the Prolegomenon] states:

"In the first volume,") Jingxi did not permit the conjoining of two distinct entities when discussing identity; rather, one must directly realize that the entity itself is entirely so, only then may it be called such.
"Immediate" (*ji*) means that the three paths are identical to the three virtues; the currents of birth-and-death and nirvana are all non-dual in essence, which is termed "immediate.
Now, below, the Fourth Ming [Zhiyi] discusses this from the perspective of the total embodiment of function, while the other schools discuss it from the perspective of mutual opposition.
Comparing their gains and losses, there are three parts: first, the other schools' doctrine of the unification of truth and falsehood, wherein the single principle accords with conditions.
The other school’s explanation below states: "Regarding the distinct principle following conditions, this section is based on the teachings and meanings of our own school.

Zongmi, in his *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (Vol. 1, Part 1), cites a passage from the Xianshou school regarding these meanings. (16) First, regarding the meaning of the essence being free from marks:
this refers to the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing, and is equal and one.

The principle of essence is without differentiation (now described as "pure unity," which is the characteristic of True Suchness); second, the meaning of arising and ceasing through following conditions, which is the Gate of Arising and Ceasing—following conditions and shifting to form the defiled and the pure;
although the defiled and the pure are formed, the nature remains eternally unmoving (now described as "differentiation," which is the characteristic of ignorance).
First, the principle itself is True Suchness and is pure; this is the "subject that follows" (the capacity to follow), while the nine realms are the "differentiation" (the objects followed).
Furthermore, [the *Suixi*] states: "To speak directly of true nature (*tathatā*), there is no differentiation;

it is only because of the differentiation of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) that one speaks of differentiation among the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*). Now, [the text] says that differentiation is the characteristic of ignorance (*avidyā*), while pure unity is the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The Commentary (*Śū*) states: "The non-arising and non-ceasing [of True Suchness] being in conjunction with arising and ceasing [of phenomena] is the gate of following conditions (*suíyuán-mén*)."
Now it is said that when following conditions there is differentiation, whereas when not following conditions there is no differentiation;

thus we know that only when the single nature combines with ignorance does differentiation arise. That is to say, when True Suchness abides in its own nature and the various phenomena of dependent origination have not yet been discussed, there is no differentiation.
Now, judging by this principle, since it is only through the union of the true and the false that [differentiation occurs],...
The ability to follow conditions precisely means that these two things are joined together; it does not mean that their essence is non-dual in the sense of mutual identity.

Regarding "the absence of differentiation when ignorance is removed": the single nature of True Suchness (tathatā) is the Buddha-realm. When it is conjoined with ignorance, there appear the differentiated characteristics of the nine realms.
If ignorance is severed, the nine realms are extinguished, and only the single nature remains. Therefore, [it is said that] there is no differentiation.

There is no distinction between these two. In our school’s teaching, the essence and function are such that the essence is identical to the principle (*li*), which constructs the three thousand [realms] as the unchanging nature;
the function is identical to phenomena, which constructs the three thousand [realms] as the following of conditions.

In our school, it is only when the entire principle-essence of the three thousand realms gives rise to the three thousand phenomenal functions through the following of conditions that this constitutes the meaning of "following conditions" in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This is complete.
In principle, phenomena are but one; the three thousand realms exist within both cultivation and nature, as essence and function.
When not following conditions, the ten realms are inherently present without lacking a single dharma; thus it is said that the three thousand realms are perfectly manifest.
Therefore, the differentiated three thousand realms of phenomenal function are non-dual with their essence. To exclude ignorance and perceive differentiation is what is called "attainment."

Excluding the cultivation of evil, it is the matter of nature; the three thousand phenomena (*trisāhasra-dharmakāya*) are created, yet their substance does not move even by a hair’s breadth. Therefore, it is said that there is a difference.

Regarding the "three proofs" (*trividha-pramāṇa*), the section below judges the doctrines of other schools as being logically untenable. As for the clarification of "identity," the Preface to the *Zangshu* states:

"Without changing its unchanging nature, it arises as dependent origination, such that defilement and purity are eternally distinct; yet without abandoning dependent origination, it is identical to the True [Suchness], such that the holy and the ordinary are one."
The *Huayan shu* states: "Because it is unchanging, it follows conditions from beginning to end; because it follows conditions, it is able to remain unchanging.
It further states: "Following conditions is precisely non-changing; because it is non-changing, it can follow conditions.

Now, in evaluating other schools, we have already refuted the nine and revealed the one, which is precisely the meaning of "separation" (*li*). There is only the name of "identity" (*ji*), but there is no actual meaning of identity.
[Commentary]:
One should know that our school distinguishes between the Perfect (yuan) and the Separate (bie) based on identity and separation; this must be investigated and examined with care.

It should be understood that when one does not discuss the inherent perfection of reality (*liju*) but speaks only of True Suchness (*zhenru*) evolving in accordance with conditions, this still remains the meaning of "separation. Therefore, the *Dīngyì jì* states: "By means of the Separate Teaching..."
Because there are nine [aspects] of the inherent nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) within the middle, both self and other sever the nine [realms].

If the three thousand worlds are the inherent nature-virtue, then the nine realms have nothing to be destroyed, as they are themselves the Buddha-dharma; thus the meaning is finally established and the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-yukti*) first becomes manifest.

Therefore, the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) states: "The meaning of transformation (*pariṇāma*) consists of only two [aspects], which is precisely the Perfect [Teaching]. Thus we know that only when both aspects of inclusion and transformation are clarified together is [the truth] fully realized.

The name itself implies that if either [nature or cultivation] is lacking, neither can be considered perfect or ultimate. Jingxi said: "Other schools do not clarify the relationship between cultivation and nature.

If one were to take the single principle of True Suchness as 'nature' and its随缘 (following conditions) manifestations as 'cultivation,' such was indeed being asserted by many people at the time when Jingxi appeared.
Thus we know that while other traditions claim to reach the ultimate perfection, they speak only of "the arising of nature" (*xingqi*) and do not speak of "nature" (*xing*) itself.

[Question: Since [the teaching] possesses that which is profoundly contemplable, yet does not discuss the inherent presence of the hundred realms (*śata-dhātu*) but instead discusses the transformation and creation of all phenomena, how can it be called "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskāra*)?

[Explanation: This is analyzed according to identity and difference, yielding three categories: first, the indication of the nine realms as being identical to the Buddha-realm, which is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*);

second, the explanation of the Buddha-realm apart from the nine realms, which is the meaning of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*); third, the refutation by others of the distinctions among the nine realms.

Returning separately to the Buddha-realm, which is of a single nature, merely attains the meaning of "separation" (li), which is precisely equivalent to the Separate Teaching (biejiao) of our own school.
One should know that the passage cited below demonstrates this meaning: one should know that other schools do not clarify the principle that all phenomena are inherently complete (lizhi).

They do not understand how the entire substance gives rise to function; they merely clarify the Single Truth and, following the conditions of the nine realms, produce differentiated phenomena—this is precisely the meaning of "separation" cited here.

The *Zhengyi Miaole* states: "Because the Separate Teaching lacks the nine [realms] of inherent nature (*xingde*), one must sever the nine for oneself and others, separately cultivating the conditions (*yuan*) and the understanding (*liao*) to manifest the originally existing, eternal Dharma-body. (Text) Since the nature does not inherently possess the nine, they must be severed; is this not the meaning of 'separation'?
As for the statement that there is nothing to be destroyed among the nine realms, it means that the transformation and creation of the nine realms is what is termed 'cultivation' (*xiu*).
The evil nature is said to be "endowed with the nine realms" because cultivation is identical to the nature; thus, there is nothing within the nine that is to be destroyed.

Although the nine are endowed within the one, and although there are distinctions such as sentient beings and Buddhas, or form and mind, taking up any one of them fully encompasses all. From the perspective of what is predominant, this refers to the Buddha’s transformations and so forth, which are categorized as being merely two.

As the *Jinbi* (Golden Needle) states: "The meaning of transformation is merely twofold. The inclusion of the term "etc. (*diǎng*) here refers to what is stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: [the three types of transformation].
The "inconceivable perfuming" and the "inconceivable transformation" are both general and specific; thus, the term "etc. is used.
To "fully clarify both transformation and [perfuming]" means that "fullness" refers to the essence of principle (*li*) and "transformation" refers to the function of phenomena (*shi*).

When one speaks of "identity" (*ji*), it must be understood as pointing to phenomena being identical to principle, practice being identical to nature, and function being entirely identical to essence; only then does it accord with the meaning of the non-duality of essence in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Third, Jingxi [Zhiyi], in his *Miaole* (The Wondrous Joy), examines the past through the present, stating: "Those who have recently read this teaching do not understand cultivation and nature" (*wen*:

"Cultivation and nature are each discussed as the three thousand [dharmas] belonging to the Perfect [Teaching]; other schools do not clarify that the single principle has distinctions, yet they discuss cultivation and nature as belonging to the Separate [Teaching].
There are even those who say it is merely 'nature-arising,' which belongs to the One Vehicle of the Perfect [Teaching] of other schools").

The teachings speak of four kinds of *dharmadhātu*: (1) the nature-reality (*svabhāva*), which is the perfect fusion of principle; (2) the dependent origination of phenomena, which is unimpeded; (3) the mutual identity and interpenetration of phenomena and principle;

and (4) the infinite interrelation of the primary and the attendant, and the environment and its inhabitants. These constitute the ultimate teaching. However, if one were to discuss them merely as transformations and creations, how could they be called "without an agent"?
It is because they transform while being fully possessed [of their own nature] that, when the nature subsumes the cultivation, they are truly termed "without an agent."
[Commentary]:
When people of the world see me establish the distinct teaching (biejiao) as having the principle of "following conditions" (suíyuán), they are bewildered and their hearts are startled;

this is because they are unable to deeply investigate the intent of Jingxi [Zhanran]. For instance, in the *Jiwen* (Commentary on the Record), while explaining the passage concerning Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya, it says:

The Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) may also be said to establish all phenomena from the "root of non-abiding" (*amūla*). Ignorance veils the principle; both the veiling agent and the veiled object are termed "non-abiding.

However, because they differ in terms of being identical or not identical [to the principle], the teachings are distinguished. Since it is granted that the veiled object is non-abiding True Suchness (*tathatā*), why would it not accord with conditions?
If it were to accord with conditions yet still not be identical [to the principle], it would be irrational; therefore, it is the "inherently complete" (*li-zu*) that accords with conditions.

It is because of conditions (*pratyaya*). Furthermore, it is said that True Suchness (*tathatā*) in its state of delusion can give rise to the nine realms; if it did not follow along with conditions, how could it give rise to the nine?

Moreover, in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), while explaining that in the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-yāna*) the faculties and objects of a single thought-moment serve as the basis for both delusion and enlightenment, it cites the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, which states:

"The Tathāgata is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome. It then provides its own commentary, stating: "This refers to the Tathāgata of the principle-nature (*li-xing*). (*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*)

This sentence is the basis upon which other schools rely regarding the principle of following conditions (*pratyaya*). To explain this meaning, [the author] cites the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise), which says:
"It is like the water in a great pond: when an elephant enters, it becomes turbid; when a pearl enters, it becomes clear.

One should know that the water is the basis for clarity and turbidity, while the pearl and the elephant are the conditions for clarity and turbidity. Based on these various passages, is it not the case that distinct principles follow conditions?

Because it is provisional, if one does not speak of the inherent possession of the essence (*tǐjù*), then whether [the mind] follows conditions or does not follow conditions, both belong to the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*).
Why is this? For instance, when it is said that "Ālaya gives rise to all dharmas," or "Dharmatā gives rise to all dharmas," are these not two meanings of the Separate Teaching?
Question: In the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), the explanation of the non-abiding of ignorance says, "It speaks of itself..."

"Abiding in this" refers to the meaning of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha/Śrāvaka), while "abiding in dependence on others" (paratantra) refers to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Mahāyāna).

Furthermore, the principle of "following conditions," wherein the true and the false are harmoniously combined to create all phenomena, is precisely what constitutes *paratantra*. This point is clearly stated in the *Commentary* (Shu): "The phrasing is concise and the meaning is profound;
one must rely upon the *Records* (Ji) for interpretation in order to reveal the definitive intent. Thus, it explains that the self-abiding nature of phenomena and afflictions mutually... [interact].
Because they are mutually established as both self and other through the bonds, both self and other lack the meaning of "perfect" (yuan).
Since the nature of delusion is determinately able to act as an obstruction, only by breaking the obstruction can one determinately manifest the principle. To explain the "dependent" (yi-ta):

they depend on one another and are identical to one another because their essence is the same; thus, it is "depending and yet identical. This concludes the distinction between the Separate (bie) and the Perfect (yuan).
The *Jiaojie* (Exposition of the Teachings) states that the two teachings are distinguished based on whether the self and others are identical or different in essence.

Our current commentary explains: the nature-essence (*xingti*) fully possesses the nine [aspects], which give rise to the nine functions of cultivation (*xiu*). These functions still rely upon the essence; thus they are called "identical essence" (*tongti*). Based on this reliance and direction, if it were otherwise, it would not accord with the meaning of "reliance" here.
Therefore, the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy) says: "In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), there are no nine aspects of nature-virtue; therefore, there is no identity between self and others."
In both cases, one must sever the nine [stages]; this shows that while it is fundamentally principle (*li*), it functions according to conditions (*yuan*) as the nine stages.
Since the function of ignorance is not non-existent, it certainly acts as an obstruction; therefore, only by breaking these nine can one manifest the principle.

If cultivation arises entirely from nature, then phenomena are identical to principle—how could they be fixed obstructions that must be broken? If you insist that it is only principle functioning according to conditions as the nine stages...

Regarding those who advocate for the "perfect" (yuan) meaning: why is it that in the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), the True Suchness (zhenru) in its state of delusion, which is capable of producing the nine realms, is judged to be distinct?
Therefore, as long as the principle of the union of the true and the false has not yet been established, it is still termed "abiding in itself.

The subsequent passage in that commentary, which analyzes the opening and closing [of the teachings], states regarding the Separate Teaching (biejiao) that it likewise "abides according to the dharma-nature" (faxing). Thus, one must investigate the underlying principle; one must not be deluded by mere names.

If this school had not been for Jingxi’s precise and concise elucidation of the perfect meaning (*yuan-yi*), it would have forever remained submerged. [Commentary: Regarding the meaning of "following conditions" (*sui-yuan*) based on the distinct principle (*bie-li*), there are three parts:
first, refuting those in the world who do not permit it; second, citing texts to establish the doctrine; third, concluding the judgment based on the texts.

As for "those in the world," this refers to the various masters of the Four Ming temples who established the distinct principle of following conditions but did not permit [the perfect teaching]; Yongjia Ji succeeded them.
Master Sili Suíyuán of Lìlàn Jiāhuó, Master Sili Suíyuán of Tiāntái Yuǎnyǐng, and Master Sili Suíyuán Zhēngjué extensively refuted my current statement.
Upon hearing these words of mine, these masters were bewildered and their hearts were struck with alarm;
this was because they were ignorant of the profound purport of Jīngxī, even though Jīngxī did not explicitly establish those specific names.

There is a principle that connects and leads through three passages to demonstrate this; the explanation of "Ajñāta" (A-ruo) is as follows. According to the first fascicle of the *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), based on the commentary (*shu*), "Ajñāta-Kauṇḍinya":
"Kauṇḍinya" is the clan name, while "Ajñāta" is the personal name. It is translated as "One Without Knowledge.

Taking the "Wisdom of Non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) as its name, it is explained according to the four teachings. Regarding the specific contemplation of non-arising wisdom, it says: "In reliance upon..."

The *Fajie xing putixing ji shi* (Commentary on the Record of the Practice of the Dharma-realm Bodhisattva Path) states: "Engaging in practice based on the object" refers specifically to taking the principle alone as the basis;

it is covered by the nine realms and serves as the supporting dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This dharma-realm is simply the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), and it is further that upon which both delusion and enlightenment depend.
Within this context, one should also say: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. Ignorance covers the principle; thus, there is both that which covers and that which is covered.

The concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and its accompaniments are both termed "non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita*); yet, by distinguishing whether they are identical to or different from [the nature], the teachings are differentiated.

Now, turning one's back on delusion to achieve awakening, one focuses exclusively on the rational nature (*dharmatā*) to shatter the nine realms (as the text states). In both the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles], the true nature is equally expounded;

since this nature does not abide fixedly, it is able to establish all phenomena, which is why the word "also" is used. In the Buddha-realm, there is only the principle, which is not identical to the nine realms, yet it is capable of... [the text here appears truncated].
If one asks whether the truth concealed [by ignorance], though entirely non-abiding, is itself the Perfect (yuan) or the Separate (bie):
it is known that the principle of "non-abiding" and True Suchness (tathatā) following conditions are identical in substance but differ in name.

Since you have already granted that the truth concealed is called the "Non-abiding Basis," is this not the Separate Principle following conditions? If it is still not identical, it is because it is not the "inherently endowed" (liju). This is because...

According to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), that which is able to follow is True Suchness; it is merely the Middle Way Buddha-nature. That which is followed consists of the phenomena of the nine realms produced by defiled conditions.
Since these nine are not intrinsically complete (xingju) but arise solely through following conditions, one must destroy the nine to reveal the one; therefore, they are not mutually identical.

In the Perfect Teaching (yuan), the ten realms are entirely the nature itself, which, following defiled or pure conditions, transforms and creates phenomenal functions. Thus, cultivation and nature are identical in essence and function.
Since Hengtong [the ninth stage] arises from cultivation while fully embodying the nature, cultivation is identical to the nature; thus, the nine stages are identical to the nature.

The subsequent passage explains that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) follows conditions while clarifying its inherent endowment (*tiji*), whereas the provisional teachings differ in that they clarify following conditions through principle alone.
That True Suchness gives rise to the nine stages is also an interpretation of the text regarding "A-ruo" (Ajñāta); it signifies that True Suchness does not abide in itself.
Because the intrinsic nature follows the conditions of ignorance, it is said to be "in delusion"; because it follows conditions, it is able to give rise to the nine realms.
It is precisely by means of this arising phenomenon that the quality of following conditions is revealed; thus it is said: "If it did not follow conditions, how could it give rise to the nine realms?

Zhuan-an [Zhi-yan] claims that Siming [Zhi-yi] falsely accused him by taking the arising phenomenon itself to be "following conditions. One must understand that True Suchness is in a state of delusion.
Right speech can follow and give rise to the nine realms; the treatise on the arising of phenomena states that phenomena arise because they follow conditions.

Regarding the auxiliary practices of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the *Zhi guan fu xing zhuan* says: "To contemplate that the single thought-moment of root and object arises is precisely the provisional name;
this mind of provisional names is the basis for both delusion and liberation. The commentary on the *Fu xing* explains: "To illuminate and know that from one mind there arise immeasurable minds."

Because the mind is immeasurable, delusion and awakening are immeasurable. Delusion constitutes the suffering and origin [of the truth] within the ten realms; awakening constitutes the path and cessation in four ways.

The fifth chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; this refers to the Tathāgata as the principle-nature (*li-xing*) being the root of both good and evil.
Accordingly, the ten realms should be understood as mutually serving as the basis for good and evil. Furthermore, it cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as follows: "As it is now..."

In the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), because the faculties, objects, and a single thought-moment (yī-niàn) are all endowed with the nature-reality of the Buddha-realm, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is cited to demonstrate that the Tathāgata of the nature-reality is realized within a single thought-moment.
Since the good serves as the realization of awakening and the non-good serves as the realization of delusion, the cause is precisely this fundamental nature.

Therefore, the single thought-moment arising from the mutual confrontation of the faculties and objects is the basis for both delusion and awakening; thus, the Tathāgata of the nature-reality is designated as "good."

The unwholesome causes follow ignorance as their condition; when nine [factors] act as delusion, one follows the teacher’s instruction, and when they act as awakening, one attains liberation—this is precisely the two-fold dependent origination of defilement and purity.
As for what other schools rely upon, Master Zang establishes the theory of "following conditions" based precisely on this text.

The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (Part One) states: "The meaning of arising and ceasing by following conditions refers to the gate of arising and ceasing; that is, following the influence [of perfuming]."
It transforms into the defiled and the pure (and so forth, leading to the citation from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*):

"The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome. Regarding the pond water and other elements: water is a metaphor for a single thought-moment; the pearl is a metaphor for pure conditions; the clarity is a metaphor for the Buddha-realm;

the elephant is a metaphor for defiled conditions; and the turbidity is a metaphor for the nine realms. This analogy applies to both the Perfect and the Separate Teachings; however, in the present text, it refers specifically to the Separate Teaching, mentioning only the "elephant entering."

Regarding the phrase "then turbidity," the subsequent passage uses the analogy of a circle to state that turbidity and water exist together; thus, one knows that the following section clarifies both the arising of phenomena (*dharmas*) and their nature.
First, it briefly excludes [the view] that does not discuss the inherent presence of the essence, then it indicates what follows and what does not follow [conditions].

Furthermore, it cites the *ālayavijñāna*’s arising of phenomena to prove they do not follow conditions, and it cites the arising of phenomena from the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) to prove they do follow conditions. If one were to speak only of the false arising [of phenomena], [it would be incomplete].

The nine realms are directly explained as the phenomena that arise; however, if one speaks of "the dharma-nature giving birth to the nine realms," this refers to the principle of following conditions.
If the dharma-nature did not follow the condition of ignorance, how could it give rise to the nine? "All" refers to the nine realms of phenomena;

when only a single realm is explained without mentioning "all," this is likewise a *siddhānta* (established tenet) taught according to the capacities of beings, depending on whether [the teaching] follows [their specific needs] or not.

According to the theoretical principle, the single reality cannot establish itself independently of delusion, nor can delusion alone be established as real; only through the conjunction of reality and delusion can phenomena be produced.

This applies equally to both the Separate (Biaobian) and Perfect (Yuan) teachings. The distinction lies simply in whether these elements are fully present or not, and whether they are identical or not.

As for the mention of the *ālaya-vijñāna* and so forth, the *Miaoxuan* states that various treatises explain the mind as the source from which all phenomena arise differently; some refer to it as the *ālaya*.

This is the true, eternal, pure consciousness that gives rise to all phenomena; or it is said that the *ālaya* is neutral (*avyākṛta*) and that ignorance gives rise to all phenomena, and so forth (as in the text).
One should know that the present statement regarding "not following" is no different from the previous statement regarding "not following conditions.
While the words are the same, the meaning differs: the present mention of "not following" refers directly to the *ālayavijñāna* itself as that which gives rise to phenomena.

Regarding the statement that one does not follow conditions, the previous remark "not following" refers to the time when True Suchness (tathatā) abides in its own nature (*svabhāva*), before the discussion of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As for the questions and answers concerning the "abiding in oneself" (*svastha*) and so forth, this cites the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, fascicle 8, section 19, which establishes a question.

According to the commentary’s explanation, both the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) vehicles each have their own and the other; the language in the *ṭīkā* is concise, and it follows each [vehicle] individually.

"Dependent and yet identical" means that they mutually depend upon one another and so forth, due to the identity or difference of their essence. In the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), the essences of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are different;
in the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao), the essences of ignorance and the nature of phenomena are identical. Now, regarding the explanation below, which comments on the meaning of the text:

first, it explains that because their essences are identical, they are dependent and yet identical; since the essences of ignorance and the nature of phenomena are identical, the whole [of the latter] is [the former].

The arising of function still relies upon the substance; thus, function is itself the substance. The nature-substance (*xingti*) possesses nine pairs of distinct [aspects], yet there is no separate nature for these nine.
The nine functions of cultivation arise based on the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

That is to say, the nine realms inherently possessed by the substance of the dharma-nature give rise to the nine functional applications of cultivating the realms of evil. These functions, in turn, rely upon the nature.
The substance of evil, like the *dharmatā*, arises from ignorance; yet the function of cultivating the purity of the Buddha-realm is entirely possessed within the substance of ignorance.
This function, in turn, relies upon the substance of the inherent goodness of nature (*prakṛti-kuśala*).

In this text, we are currently speaking from the perspective of the conditions of the nine realms; although there is a distinction between the nine and the one regarding inherent goodness and inherent evil, [they are nonetheless one].

All are fused and obliterated; by raising one, the whole is encompassed, and thus they are collectively termed the "Essence" (*tattva*). When contrasted with the distinct [teachings], however, only nine are discussed.

If one does not provide a further explanation below, the delusions of the distinct teaching are fixed as obstacles, whereas the meaning of the distinct [nature] being devoid of inherent nature reveals that the circular nature possesses the nine [realms] within its essence.

By severing the nine [delusions] of self and others, the circular non-severance is revealed; this principle within the midst [of the distinct teaching] is able to follow defiled conditions and manifest as the nine realms.
The Dharma is entirely the work of ignorance; that is, when True Suchness (Tathatā) is in a state of delusion, it can give rise to the nine realms.

Furthermore, since it is the power of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) conjoined with the power of ignorance that creates all defiled phenomena, these phenomena do not arise from the nature itself as its inherent essence, nor do they arise from the nature alone.

Therefore, they are not called "unconditioned" (anabhisaṃskṛta). Because the nature of the afflictions of ignorance is definitively able to act as an obstruction, one must destroy the nine [realms] to reveal the Buddha.

The realms (*dhātu*) are merely principle (*li*). If one speaks of "the whole nature arising as cultivation" and so forth, this again refers to the meaning of perfection (*yuan*): the entire substance follows conditions, and the entire nature arises as cultivation.

This refers to the phenomena that follow conditions as being precisely the unchanging nature; only then can it be called "unconditioned" (*wu zuo*). Since hindrances are identical with virtues, they need not be severed.

This reveals the distinct teaching (*bie jiao*), which definitely requires breaking through [hindrances] to reveal [virtues]. If one clings to the lower [teachings], this answers the previous question.
If it is argued that "principle merely accords with conditions to form the meaning of 'round' (perfect)," how can this withstand the text of the *Miaole*?

Since it is granted that the fusion of the true and the false is precisely what constitutes the creation of all phenomena, this is indeed the meaning of "conjunction" (*he*). It results in two distinct dharmas each abiding in itself;
it is not the meaning of "identity" (*ji*). Therefore, it is said that the analysis of "opening and closing" has not yet been finalized. (From the *Jingming shu*, Fascicle 8 [10])
